CAISI signed new agreements with Google DeepMind, Microsoft and xAI in May 2026, joining OpenAI and Anthropic.
keys: voluntary access agreements with CAISI
the June 2026 executive order calls for a voluntary early-access framework
no mandatory testing law has passed
items.x: Executive Order 14409 (June 2, 2026) calls for a voluntary framework giving the government access to covered models up to 30 days before developers release them to other trusted partners, and says it does not authorize mandatory licensing or preclearance. Mandatory proposals include the AI Risk Evaluation Act, run by the Department of Energy, and Sen. Mark Warner's Artificial Intelligence Risk Management and Security Act (S. 5576), which would give a new AI Safety Board access 45 days before release.

items.p: Under a 'regulatory markets' approach, why would government certify private verifiers of AI safety instead of writing detailed technical rules itself?
items.answer: Legislators and agencies lack the technical staff and speed to turn safety goals into detailed rules for fast-changing AI. Certified private verifiers can build that expertise and update their methods faster, while government sets the goals and licenses and oversees the verifiers.
keys: government lacks technical expertise and speed
private verifiers build expertise and update methods faster
government sets the goals and polices the verifiers
items.x: The idea comes from Gillian Hadfield and Jack Clark, who propose that governments require regulated companies to buy oversight services from government-licensed private regulators, so market incentives develop the technical methods while government sets priorities. California's SB 813 (signed September 9, 2026) borrows part of the idea in voluntary form: a state agency designates independent verification organizations (IVOs) and can suspend or end a designation.

choice.p: What is the core argument for having government certify private AI safety verifiers?
o: Private verifiers adapt faster, while government sets the goals and polices them
Private verifiers can legally block model releases, which government agencies cannot do
It lets each lab set its own safety goals, with no government involvement at all
It replaces lawsuits as the only way to hold AI developers accountable
ow: Government agencies can also hold power to block releases, as under licensing; the case for verifiers rests on expertise and speed.
Government sets the goals in this model; labs don't choose their own standards.
These proposals leave lawsuits in place; some make verification count in court.

items.p: Under voluntary certified-verifier laws and proposals, such as California's SB 813, developers don't have to get verified. What do these designs offer developers as a reason to opt in?
items.answer: Help in court. If the developer is later sued over harms, having passed verification can count in its defense, ranging from evidence that counts but doesn't decide the case (SB 813 as enacted) to a full defense against liability in some proposals.
keys: a benefit in later lawsuits or liability protection
works as an incentive in place of a mandate
items.x: As enacted in September 2026, SB 813 says an audit done under the state's standards is "relevant to, but not conclusive of" a lawsuit over AI harms. Its 2025 version went further, offering certified developers an affirmative defense. Not every verifier design is voluntary: Hadfield and Clark's original "regulatory markets" idea would require companies to buy oversight, and the federal FRONTIER Act bill would require the very largest developers to retain a licensed verifier.

choice.p: In voluntary certified-verifier (IVO) designs like California's SB 813, what draws developers to opt in?
o: Legal protection or favorable weight if they are later sued over harms
An exemption from every state AI safety law that would otherwise apply
Permission to skip government safety testing before each release
A waiver from having to publish their safety frameworks
ow: Broad exemptions from state laws come from federal preemption, a separate fight.
IVO proposals don't waive pre-release testing; they add a separate check.
Verification builds on published frameworks; it doesn't waive them.

items.p: Certified private verifiers: government certifies private organizations to check AI developers' safety, often with legal benefits for developers who pass. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: when developers choose and pay their own verifiers, competition pushes verifiers toward leniency (Gabriel Weil); policing verifiers still takes public experts able to second-guess them (Weil); the verifier market will take years to build, while the FRONTIER Act's preemption of state laws would be immediate (ARI); legal benefits could shield developers who pass a lenient check.
keys: developer-paid verifiers compete on leniency
government still needs its own experts to police the verifiers
the verifier market and standards don't exist yet
the legal benefit could become a shield
preemption could take effect before the verifier market exists
items.x: Weil's proposed fix is mandatory liability insurance, so whoever judges the risk also bears the cost of misses. ARI, which supports verifiers, would keep government examiners doing a share of reviews so they can check verifiers' findings against their own. Among SB 813's criteria for designating verifiers: a verifier can't accept pay that depends on the results of its assessment.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to certified private verifiers?
o: Verifiers chosen and paid by developers face pressure to be lenient
Verifiers would give the government power to decide which labs may operate
Verifiers can test models only through the public interface everyone uses
Verification would make developers liable for every harm their models cause
ow: That is an objection to licensing, which verifier systems don't create.
Access depends on the design; the FRONTIER Act would give verifiers unredacted materials.
Verification usually reduces developers' legal exposure; it doesn't expand it.

items.p: Even with a mature market of private AI verifiers, which job might government need to keep for itself?
o: Judging whether a developer's safety measures are adequate
Writing each developer's safety framework for it
Setting the fees that developers must pay their verifiers
Running every model test itself, with no private help at all
ow: Developers write their own frameworks in this design; government examines them.
Fee-setting isn't the job reserved for government; the one never handed off is judging adequacy.
These designs use accredited private verifiers alongside government examiners.
keys: government keeps the final judgment of whether safety measures are adequate
items.x: This is the position of the August 2026 blueprint from ARI (Americans for Responsible Innovation), which says the government "never fully relinquishes" its duty to judge whether developers' frameworks meet federal minimum standards. The government would also direct for-cause examinations, inspect verifiers' work, and do a share of examinations itself so it has a baseline for judging verifiers' findings.

items.p: What do supporters say a license to build or release frontier AI models can do that disclosure rules and liability can't?
items.answer: Act before harm. Disclosure and liability work after the fact, while a license lets government stop a dangerous model before it is built or shipped, and the threat of losing a license gives the regulator strong leverage over a few high-value companies.
keys: stops dangerous models before training or release
disclosure and liability act after the fact
the threat of revocation gives leverage
items.x: The strongest versions make the license depend on meeting safety standards and passing review, with the power to revoke it. The 2023 Blumenthal-Hawley framework proposed licensing by an independent oversight body; Sen. Bernie Sanders's Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act (2026) would require a federal charter to develop advanced models and approval before each deployment.

choice.p: What do supporters say licensing can do that disclosure rules and liability cannot?
o: Stop a dangerous model before anyone builds or releases it
Make developers pay compensation after an AI system has harmed someone
Let the public read each lab's safety plans, test results and incident reports
Check once a year whether each lab follows the safety plan it published
ow: Compensating victims after the fact is what liability does.
Public visibility into safety plans is what disclosure rules provide.
Checking adherence to a lab's own plan is a third-party audit.

items.p: New York and Illinois have enacted laws requiring large frontier developers to register with the state, starting in 2027. How does registration differ from licensing, and what is it for?
items.answer: Registration means filing basic facts (in Illinois: identity, offices, major owners and contacts) and paying a fee; there's no safety review or approval. Its main use is giving regulators a list of who is building frontier models so other rules can reach them. A license makes permission depend on meeting safety standards and can be revoked.
keys: no approval or safety review needed
purpose: know who the frontier developers are so other rules can reach them
licensing makes permission depend on safety and can be revoked
items.x: From January 1, 2027, Illinois's SB 315 bars large frontier developers from developing, deploying or operating a frontier model in the state without a current disclosure statement and fee; the statement lists identity, offices, major owners and contacts. New York's RAISE Act office at the Department of Financial Services is set to start registering developers in November 2026.

choice.p: How does the registration New York and Illinois require differ from licensing?
o: Developers file basic facts like ownership; there's no safety review or approval
Developers must pass a government safety test before each model release
Developers must hire an outside auditor before they are allowed to register at all
Registration can be revoked whenever a model fails a government safety review
ow: A pass-or-fail test before release is closer to licensing or mandatory testing.
Audits are a separate duty (Illinois requires them from 2028); registering needs no auditor.
Revocation after a failed review is a feature of licensing, which registration lacks.

items.p: Licensing: frontier developers would need government permission before training or releasing top models. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: approval fits poorly because the regulated product is hard to define and its harms are uncertain (Daniel Carpenter and Carson Ezell, Harvard); it raises costs for smaller and open-source developers and invites capture by incumbents who help write the rules; it gives officials broad discretion over who may build or release AI; it slows useful releases.
keys: raises entry costs or entrenches incumbents (regulatory capture)
hard to define what's licensed or judge safety
too much executive discretion or power
slows beneficial releases
items.x: The current White House has kept clear of licensing: President Trump's June 2026 executive order says nothing in it authorizes mandatory licensing, preclearance or permitting of AI models. Carpenter and Ezell don't rule approval out; they argue that a simple copy of FDA-style approval would fit frontier AI poorly.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to licensing frontier AI developers?
o: It entrenches big incumbents and burdens smaller and open-source developers
It only checks paperwork, so labs can pass while ignoring the real risks
It acts only after harm has happened, too late to prevent it
It depends on labs volunteering, so reckless labs can simply opt out
ow: The paperwork worry is aimed at compliance audits; licensing can require real safety review.
Acting too late is the critique of liability and disclosure, which licensing is meant to answer.
Voluntariness is the critique of current pre-release testing; a license is mandatory.

items.p: As of October 2026, how far has frontier AI licensing gone in the US?
o: Only registration is law, in New York and Illinois; approval licensing is only in bills
Congress enacted the 2023 Blumenthal-Hawley licensing framework, run by an independent board
A June 2026 executive order requires Commerce licenses for models above a compute threshold
California requires a state license to train any model above its SB 53 threshold
ow: The Blumenthal-Hawley framework was a 2023 proposal and was never enacted.
Executive Order 14409 says the opposite: nothing in it authorizes mandatory licensing, preclearance or permitting.
SB 53 requires published frameworks and transparency reports; it has no licensing step for training.
keys: only registration is enacted (New York, Illinois)
approval-based licensing exists only in bills
items.x: Registration in both states takes effect in 2027. One far-reaching licensing bill is Sen. Sanders's Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act (September 2026), which would require a federal charter to develop or distribute advanced models and approval before each deployment, with charters revocable for violations.

items.p: Why do supporters argue a dedicated frontier AI regulator is needed even if audits, testing and certified verifiers exist?
items.answer: Every other tool needs someone with expertise and authority to run it. US frontier oversight is spread across voluntary CAISI testing, state attorneys general and agencies with no AI mandate, so no one can act quickly. A dedicated body could keep thresholds current, build technical staff and enforce rules consistently.
keys: other tools need an institution to run and enforce them
oversight is fragmented; no one has both expertise and authority
could update rules, build staff and enforce consistently
items.x: Designs range from a new agency to an office inside an existing one. New York put its RAISE Act office (called DIGIT) inside the Department of Financial Services, and the EU's AI Office gained powers to enforce its rules for general-purpose AI models on August 2, 2026.

choice.p: What gap do supporters say a dedicated frontier AI regulator would fill?
o: No US body has the expertise and power to oversee frontier AI
No federal agency currently tests frontier models for dangerous capabilities at all
Courts have no power to hear lawsuits over harms caused by AI systems
No state requires frontier AI labs to publish any safety information
ow: CAISI already tests models, though only voluntarily.
Courts can hear AI-related lawsuits under existing law.
California's SB 53 already requires large developers to publish safety frameworks.

items.p: Match each proposal or law to the kind of AI oversight body it would create.
pairs: Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act
A new Department of Artificial Intelligence led by its own Secretary
Warner's AI Risk Management and Security Act
A board inside Commerce with access to new models 45 days before release
FRONTIER Act
A new Commerce Under Secretary who licenses and oversees private verifiers
New York's RAISE Act
A state office inside the Department of Financial Services
items.x: The options run from a brand-new department to an office inside an existing agency. A body inside Commerce could build on NIST and CAISI. In September 2026 Sen. Ted Cruz blocked a bid to pass Warner's bill by unanimous consent, saying it would put too much authority in the hands of the board and the Commerce Department.

items.p: Dedicated AI regulator: Congress or a state creates a body to set and enforce frontier AI safety rules. Name two objections or risks critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: it puts too much authority in one board or agency (Sen. Ted Cruz's objection to Warner's AI Safety Board bill); without a budget or investigative powers it may exist only on paper (Dan Parshall, calling the FRONTIER Act's Under Secretary "an at-will appointee with no budget"); it can be captured by industry or used politically to favor or punish particular labs.
keys: too much agency or executive discretion
a paper regulator without funding, staff, subpoena power or Senate confirmation
capture by industry or political misuse
underfunding
items.x: Parshall notes the FRONTIER Act's Under Secretary would be appointed by the Commerce Secretary without Senate confirmation, that the bill appropriates no money, and that it grants no subpoena power. Underfunding already affects today's testing body: IFP (May 2026) estimates CAISI needs at least 84 million dollars a year, against a current budget of about 15 million.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to a dedicated frontier AI regulator?
o: Without funding and investigative powers, it may exist only on paper
It relies on labs volunteering, so reckless labs can simply opt out
It only checks whether labs follow their own published safety plans
It shifts all oversight to private firms that the labs themselves pay
ow: Voluntariness is the critique of current pre-release testing; a regulator has legal authority.
That is the limit of compliance audits.
Lab-paid private oversight is the worry about certified verifiers.

items.p: As of October 2026, where do efforts to create a dedicated federal regulator for frontier AI stand in the US?
o: New York set up a registration office; no federal regulator bill has passed
Congress created a Department of AI when it passed the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act
The Senate passed Warner's AI Safety Board bill by unanimous consent in September 2026
NIST’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation gained enforcement powers over frontier labs in 2026
ow: The Ban ASI Act is a 2026 bill from Sen. Sanders and Rep. Greg Casar; it has not passed.
Sen. Ted Cruz objected to Warner's unanimous consent request, which blocked it.
CAISI tests models and develops standards; it has no power to enforce rules on developers.
keys: New York's DFS office is set to register developers
federal regulator bills have not passed
items.x: New York's DIGIT office in the Department of Financial Services is set to start registering developers in November 2026, with RAISE Act compliance from January 2027. Federally, Cruz blocked a quick vote on Warner's AI Safety Board bill, and the FRONTIER Act, which would create a Commerce Under Secretary, had not moved past committee referral.

items.p: Match each verification tool to the main failure it targets.
pairs: Third-party audit
A lab quietly skips the safety practices it published
Embedded evaluators
Warning signs appear during training or internal use, out of outsiders' view
Government pre-release testing
A new model has dangerous capabilities the lab missed or underweighted
Certified private verifiers
Government lacks the expertise and speed to write detailed technical rules
Licensing
A dangerous model gets built or shipped before anyone can stop it
Dedicated AI regulator
No one has both the expertise and the authority to run oversight
items.x: One way to see how they fit together: audits, verifiers and embedded evaluators check what labs claim and do; testing checks the models themselves; licensing and a regulator supply the power to act on bad findings.

items.p: A legislator worries that a lab has been using an unreleased model inside the company for months to speed up its own AI research, and that outsiders would never notice. Which tool is designed for this problem?
o: Embedded evaluators with ongoing, employee-like access inside the lab
An annual third-party audit checking the lab's published safety framework
Government safety testing of each model shortly before its public release
A registration requirement listing the lab's owners and offices
ow: A yearly audit checks adherence to the framework and may never see live internal use.
Pre-release testing is triggered by a public release, which a model used only internally may never reach.
Registration tells regulators who the lab is and reveals nothing about its internal work.
keys: embedded evaluators
ongoing inside access to see internal use
items.x: Internal use is the case embedded assessments were designed for: GovAI's proposal stresses that risks from frontier AI depend on how developers use and govern systems internally. California's September 2026 executive order asks whether to require onsite verifiers at large labs.

items.p: A state wants expert, independent checks on frontier labs but has almost no technical staff and doesn't want to impose a mandate yet. Which tool best fits?
o: Certified private verifiers that developers can opt into for a legal benefit
A state licensing board that approves each new model before its release
A new state agency staffed to examine frontier labs directly
Embedded state inspectors required by law at every large lab
ow: Licensing is a mandate and needs expert reviewers the state lacks.
A staffed agency is exactly the capacity the state doesn't have yet.
A required onsite inspector is a mandate, and the state would need experts to fill the role.
keys: certified private verifiers (IVOs)
voluntary opt-in with a legal benefit
items.x: This is roughly the approach California took with SB 813 (2026): a state agency designates verification organizations and developers choose whether to use them. Critics such as Gabriel Weil warn that verifiers chosen by developers are pushed toward leniency, and that policing verifiers still takes public expertise.

items.p: A lab passes its annual audit with no findings, yet outside experts think its safety framework is far too weak. Which design would most directly address that gap?
o: An outside verifier that judges if the safeguards are adequate
A more frequent compliance audit that checks the same framework every quarter
A registration rule requiring the lab to list its owners and contacts
A voluntary pledge from the lab to follow its framework more carefully
ow: Auditing the same framework more often still never asks whether it is strong enough.
Registration identifies the lab; it says nothing about the quality of its safeguards.
The lab already follows its framework; the problem is the framework itself.
keys: an assessment of whether safeguards are adequate
goes beyond compliance with the lab's own framework
items.x: Compliance audits ask whether the lab did what it said; adequacy assessments ask whether what it said is enough. The FRONTIER Act bill would require the very largest developers to retain licensed verifiers that judge whether they achieve "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation," and it also directs rules setting minimum requirements for frameworks.

units.title: Liability, incentives and lab governance
units.desc: Tools that use lawsuits, insurance, legal shields, insider reporting, antitrust law and corporate structure to change how AI labs weigh safety.

items.p: A statutory duty of care would require frontier AI developers to take reasonable care to avoid causing or enabling catastrophic harm, enforced through lawsuits. What failure do supporters say it addresses?
items.answer: Commercial and competitive pressure pushes labs to skip safety work, while much of the harm their models could cause would fall on other people. Legal exposure for careless conduct makes those precautions effectively mandatory, so lawyers and boards treat them as required.
keys: competitive or commercial pressure leads labs to skip safety work
much of the harm would fall on others, so labs underinvest in precautions
legal exposure makes precautions effectively mandatory
items.x: 'Reasonable care' is the negligence standard: a developer is liable only if it failed to act as a careful developer would and that failure caused the harm. Gabriel Weil says liability puts 'a thumb on the other side of the scale' against labs' financial incentives to push ahead. California's vetoed SB 1047 (2024) would have let the state attorney general sue developers that failed to comply.

choice.p: What failure do supporters say a statutory duty of care for frontier developers addresses?
o: Labs under competitive pressure skip safety work whose harms would fall on others
Victims of AI harms cannot tell which company built the model that hurt them
Developers cannot pay for huge harms, so their victims go uncompensated
Employees who spot dangers stay silent for fear of retaliation by the lab
ow: That is a tracing problem; a duty of care assumes the developer is known.
That is the 'judgment-proof' problem that insurance mandates target.
That is the gap whistleblower protections target.

items.p: Why do supporters of a duty of care prefer a general 'reasonable care' standard to a detailed list of required safety practices written into law?
items.answer: It is flexible: courts can judge new or unforeseen harm pathways (such as internal deployment, weak security of model weights or open release) case by case, so lawmakers don't have to anticipate every risk in advance.
keys: flexible standard
courts judge new or unforeseen harm pathways case by case
lawmakers don't need to anticipate every risk in advance
items.x: Legal scholar Ketan Ramakrishnan offers a qualified defense of negligence for foundation models, arguing that only it is broad enough to reach pathways like internal deployment, weak model-weight security and open-source release. He also proposes that courts, without any statute, widen the duty of care to cover AI behavior that would break important laws or norms if a human did it.

choice.p: Why do supporters of a duty of care prefer a general 'reasonable care' standard to a detailed list of required safety practices?
o: Courts judge new harm pathways case by case, so lawmakers needn't foresee every risk
It makes developers pay for all harms, even after taking every precaution
It gives developers a clear checklist of practices that guarantees immunity from lawsuits
It moves enforcement from the courts to a new federal AI safety agency
ow: That describes strict liability; under negligence, a developer that took reasonable care is not liable.
That describes a safe harbor; a general standard is less predictable than a checklist.
A duty of care is enforced mainly through courts and attorneys general.

items.p: A legal duty of care for frontier developers would be judged by a negligence standard in court (liable only for failing to take reasonable care). Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: unless victims can name a precaution the developer skipped, it escapes liability, so negligence misses risks no one yet knows how to prevent (Gabriel Weil, who prefers strict liability); fear of lawsuits can discourage labs from investigating and disclosing new risks (noted even by negligence defender Ketan Ramakrishnan); a true catastrophe comes too late and exceeds any firm's assets.
keys: careful developers escape liability, so risks no one can yet prevent go unpriced
discourages investigating or disclosing risks
too late and too small for a real catastrophe
items.x: Weil argues that when no one knows how to build safe systems, it is hard to name a precaution that would have prevented the harm. Ramakrishnan concludes that tort liability is inadequate on its own and calls for 'a robust regime of ex ante regulation' (rules applied before deployment) alongside it.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to a negligence-based duty of care for frontier AI developers?
o: Careful developers escape liability, so risks no one can yet prevent go unpriced
It makes developers pay for harms even when they took every possible precaution
It requires a new federal agency to write detailed safety rules for every lab
It protects developers from lawsuits as long as they publish a safety plan
ow: That describes strict liability, which critics of negligence such as Gabriel Weil prefer.
A duty of care is enforced through courts, which is why supporters call it flexible.
That describes a liability safe harbor, which works in the opposite direction.

items.p: California's SB 1047 (2024) would have required developers of very large AI models to take 'reasonable care' to avoid severe harms. What happened to it?
o: Gov. Gavin Newsom vetoed it in September 2024
It became law and took effect in January 2025
A federal court blocked it as preempted by federal law
It died in committee without a floor vote
ow: It never became law; California's later frontier law, SB 53 (2025), centers on transparency and safety frameworks.
It never took effect, so no court ruled on it.
It passed the legislature before reaching the governor.
keys: vetoed by Gov. Newsom
September 2024
items.x: Newsom vetoed it on Sept. 29, 2024, saying it applied stringent standards even to basic functions regardless of how risky the setting was. In September 2026, press reports described a Senate draft negotiated by Sens. Thune, Cruz and Klobuchar requiring developers to design products to prevent catastrophic risks; as an aide described it, companies would run their own safety tests and submit results to the Commerce secretary. Semafor reported on Sept. 29, 2026 that the talks had stalled.

items.p: Product-liability proposals would let people harmed by an AI system sue its developer over a defective design or missing warnings. How do supporters say exposure to these lawsuits makes AI safer?
items.answer: Developers expect to pay for harms their systems cause others, so they have a financial reason to invest in safer design, testing and warnings before release. The developer, who knows the system best, chooses which precautions to take, so no regulator has to specify them.
keys: developers bear the cost of harms they cause others
financial reason to invest in safer design, testing and warnings
the developer chooses the precautions; no regulator has to specify them
items.x: Economists call this internalizing an externality: making whoever creates a risk pay its costs. Sen. Dick Durbin said his AI LEAD Act 'will force AI companies to develop their products with safety in mind.'

choice.p: How do supporters say letting people sue AI developers over defective products makes AI safer?
o: Developers expect to pay for harms, so they invest in safer design
Lawsuits give regulators the evidence they need to license each model
Court settlements fund a public agency that inspects AI developers
Developers must buy insurance, and their insurers then inspect the labs
ow: Product liability works through private lawsuits; it creates no licensing system.
Damages go to injured people; funding an agency is a different policy.
That describes an insurance mandate, a separate tool often paired with liability.

items.p: Some legal scholars want strict liability for advanced AI in place of negligence. What does strict liability change, and why might it matter when no one yet knows how to make AI systems safe?
items.answer: Under strict liability the developer pays for harm its system causes even if it took every known precaution; victims need not prove carelessness. When safety methods don't exist yet, negligence lets a careful developer off, while strict liability still gives it a reason to slow down, deploy less, or invent new safeguards.
keys: developer pays even if it took every known precaution
victims need not prove carelessness or a skipped precaution
keeps a reason to slow down or find new safeguards when no known fix exists
items.x: Gabriel Weil, a leading advocate, argues that training and deploying advanced AI should count as an 'abnormally dangerous activity', a category (blasting with explosives is the classic example) where courts already apply strict liability because the activity is risky even with reasonable care. He notes that negligence usually doesn't ask whether you should have done the risky activity at all, while strict liability gives a lab a reason to wait when it isn't confident a system is safe.

choice.p: Some legal scholars favor strict liability over negligence for advanced AI. What does strict liability change?
o: The developer pays for harm its system causes, even after every known precaution
The developer pays only if victims prove in court that it failed to take reasonable care
The developer is immune if it followed a government-approved safety plan
Liability shifts from the developer to the user who prompted the model
ow: That describes negligence, the standard strict liability replaces.
That describes a liability safe harbor.
Strict liability proposals target the developer; shifting blame to users is a different choice.

items.p: One proposal would add punitive damages (extra damages on top of the victim's actual losses) in cases where AI causes smaller, compensable harm, even without malice or recklessness. What problem is this meant to solve?
o: A catastrophe would bankrupt the developer, so its cost must be charged in smaller cases
Juries tend to award too little when software, rather than a person, causes harm
Victims often cannot tell which company's model caused their particular injury
Small developers would otherwise escape the lawsuits that large labs routinely face
ow: The rationale is catastrophic risk that liability could never charge for; jury bias plays no part.
Tracing causation is a real challenge, but punitive damages do nothing to solve it.
The proposal targets advanced AI developers generally, with no special focus on small firms.
keys: a catastrophe would exceed what any company could pay
so the worst outcomes would never be charged through liability
add the expected cost of catastrophic risk to awards in smaller, payable cases
items.x: The proposal is legal scholar Gabriel Weil's. His diagnosis is that most expected harm from advanced AI lies in catastrophes where compensation would not be feasible, so ordinary liability never charges for it. Punitive damages would 'pull forward' that expected cost into near-miss cases that courts can handle. Because current doctrine requires malice or recklessness for punitive damages, Weil thinks legislation is a likelier route than the courts.

items.p: The AI LEAD Act (S. 2937, Sens. Durbin and Hawley) would treat AI systems as products, with strict liability for defects. Name two objections critics raise to product or strict liability for AI.
items.answer: Examples: the First Amendment may protect much AI output as speech, limiting some claims (Eugene Volokh); what counts as a 'defect' is unclear for AI, whose behavior depends on data, prompts and setting (Jamie Lanphear of Reed Smith); courts have traditionally treated software as a service rather than a product (Lanphear); a true catastrophe would exceed what any firm could pay (Gabriel Weil).
keys: First Amendment limits on liability for AI output
'defect' is unclear for AI software
courts have treated software as a service rather than a product
can't compensate or deter a true catastrophe
items.x: Volokh argues AI output is likely protected speech, though defamation and some other claims can still apply. At a Senate subcommittee hearing on AI agent attacks reported Oct. 1, 2026, Sen. Josh Hawley called AI systems 'a product', and witness Paul Ohm urged strict liability for AI developers. As of October 2026, the AI LEAD Act's last action is its September 2025 referral to the Judiciary Committee.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to product or strict liability for AI developers?
o: The First Amendment may protect AI output as speech, blocking some claims
It lets developers escape liability simply by following standard industry practice
It gives labs a legal shield in exchange for publishing their own safety plans
It lets rival labs coordinate their releases without antitrust review
ow: That is a critique of negligence, which strict liability is meant to fix.
That describes a liability safe harbor, the opposite approach.
That concerns an antitrust safe harbor, a different tool.

items.p: Many AI products come with terms of service that limit the company's liability. What would the AI LEAD Act (S. 2937) do about such clauses?
o: Make terms that waive rights or unreasonably limit liability unenforceable
Allow them only if the limits are disclosed in plain language before the user agrees
Cap the developer's liability at the amount the customer paid
Allow them for business customers but bar them for consumers
ow: The bill voids such clauses; disclosure does not save them.
The bill sets no cap tied to the price paid.
The bill covers both contracts with deployers and general terms and conditions.
keys: makes liability-limiting terms unenforceable
covers clauses that waive rights or unreasonably limit liability
items.x: Section 201 bars developers from contract or terms-of-service language that waives rights or unreasonably limits liability. The bill also lets individuals, classes, and the US and state attorneys general sue, and lets states pass stronger protections. Durbin and Hawley introduced it on Sept. 29, 2025.

items.p: Some proposals would require frontier developers to carry liability insurance or other financial assurance sized to the harm their models could cause. Name two things supporters say this adds to liability alone.
items.answer: (1) Victims get paid even when the harm exceeds what the developer can pay (it is 'judgment-proof'), which keeps liability credible. (2) Premiums put a price on risk before harm occurs, so riskier models cost more to deploy. (3) Insurers monitor developers, demand safety practices and lobby for stricter rules. (4) A model could be deployed only if someone will insure it.
keys: pays victims even when the developer can't (judgment-proof)
keeps liability credible for very large harms
premiums price risk, so riskier models cost more to deploy
insurers monitor developers and demand safety practices
deployment depends on finding an insurer
items.x: 'Judgment-proof' means a defendant can't pay what a court awards, so the threat of liability loses force. Cristian Trout argues insurers would model risk, monitor developers, lobby for stricter rules and advise on preventing losses. Gabriel Weil suggests a regulator could set required coverage by the worst harm a system might cause, so a model deploys only if an insurer will write an affordable policy.

choice.p: What do supporters say an insurance mandate adds to liability alone?
o: Victims get paid even if the developer can't, and insurers police safety
Developers get a legal shield from all lawsuits once they buy a qualifying insurance policy
A government fund replaces private lawsuits as the way victims are compensated
Insurers take over writing the safety rules that regulators would otherwise set
ow: Insurance pays claims; victims can still sue.
Mandates rely on private insurers; a government fund is a different design.
Insurers influence safety through pricing and policy conditions; they gain no rulemaking power.

items.p: A nuclear-style liability regime for AI catastrophes, modeled on how US nuclear power is insured, would pair mandatory insurance with what kind of liability rule?
o: Liability that is strict, capped, and assigned only to the developer
Unlimited liability shared by every company that uses the model
Government ownership of the most dangerous models
A ban on deployment until an insurer approves each model
ow: A nuclear-style regime caps liability and channels it to the developer, so insurers know the most they could owe.
The regime keeps developers private and responsible for their own liability.
Insurers price and monitor risk; they get no formal veto.
keys: strict liability (no need to prove fault)
capped (limited) liability
liability channeled only to the developer
items.x: Cristian Trout (2024) proposes this model. In his terms, liability is 'limited' (capped), 'strict' (no need to prove fault) and 'exclusive' (only the developer can be sued). In US nuclear power, the Price-Anderson Act requires $500 million of private coverage per reactor site, backed by an industry pool that can assess each reactor about $158 million more.

items.p: An insurance mandate would require frontier developers to carry coverage sized to the harms their models could cause. Name two objections or limits critics point to.
items.answer: Examples: insurers may be unable to price rare, correlated catastrophic AI risk, and some have sought to exclude AI claims; if coverage isn't for sale, a mandate either blocks deployment or needs a government backstop that shifts risk to taxpayers; a liability cap, as in Trout's nuclear-style model, limits what victims of the largest harms can recover; insurance is no substitute for regulation.
keys: insurers can't price rare, correlated catastrophic risk
if no coverage exists: deployment is blocked or taxpayers back it
a paired liability cap limits what victims recover
no substitute for regulation
items.x: Even supporter Cristian Trout calls his liability-and-insurance approach 'not a substitute for regulation'. A July 2026 GovAI paper by Trout and colleagues says insurers' exposure to AI agent risk is largely unpriced today, and that large-limit AI coverage by 2030 requires industry-wide work on incident data, catastrophe modeling and standards.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to requiring frontier developers to carry liability insurance?
o: Insurers may not be able to price rare, correlated AI catastrophes at all
It would let developers escape liability by following industry practice
It would let rival labs coordinate on pausing without antitrust review
It would make developers pay even for harms they could not have prevented
ow: That is a critique of negligence-based duties of care.
That concerns an antitrust safe harbor.
That is an objection to strict liability; insurance spreads costs without changing who is liable.

items.p: In late 2025, major US insurers such as Great American and W. R. Berkley responded to growing AI risk. What were they doing?
o: Asking US regulators to let them exclude AI claims
Launching dedicated catastrophe policies for frontier AI labs
Lobbying Congress to pass a mandatory AI insurance law
Forming a federally backed reinsurance pool for AI losses
ow: The move ran the other way: insurers sought to limit their AI exposure.
No push for a mandate was reported; the insurers sought to narrow their AI exposure.
No such pool was reported; the insurers sought to limit what they would pay for AI losses.
keys: sought regulators' permission to exclude AI-related claims
to limit their exposure to AI losses
items.x: The Financial Times reported the filings in November 2025. An underwriter told the FT that AI outputs are 'too much of a black box', and insurers feared many correlated claims at once: Aon's Kevin Kalinich said the industry could absorb a single $400 million loss but not thousands of claims from one AI provider's error. AIG, also named in reports, said it had no plans to use such exclusions. The episode illustrates a doubt about insurance mandates: coverage might not be for sale.

items.p: A liability safe harbor protects a developer from some lawsuits if it meets set conditions, such as publishing a safety plan or passing a certified audit. Why do supporters prefer this to safety mandates or ordinary lawsuits?
items.answer: It uses legal certainty as a reward: firms adopt safety practices voluntarily to earn protection, which supporters say spreads good practice faster than mandates, rewards firms that accept outside verification, and spares them inconsistent standards set by many different juries.
keys: legal certainty works as a reward for adopting safety practices
spreads good practice faster or more flexibly than mandates
rewards accepting outside verification
avoids inconsistent standards from many juries
items.x: 'Safe harbor' is a legal term for conditions that, if met, protect you from a penalty or lawsuit. It can be full immunity, a defense the developer raises in court, or a presumption that it met the standard of care. Dean Ball has proposed government-certified private auditors, with a liability safe harbor as one possible reward for certified labs.

choice.p: Why do supporters prefer a liability safe harbor to safety mandates or ordinary lawsuits?
o: Firms adopt safety practices to earn legal certainty, without rigid mandates
It raises the damages for AI harms, so firms fear lawsuits more than they do now
It lets labs coordinate release pauses without facing antitrust lawsuits
It moves all AI lawsuits into a single specialized federal court
ow: A safe harbor reduces liability exposure; it does not raise damages.
That describes an antitrust safe harbor, which shields coordination from competition law.
Safe harbors set conditions for protection; they don't change which court hears cases.

items.p: Compare two safe harbors: one shields any developer that publishes its own safety plan; the other shields only developers certified by an approved independent auditor. Why do supporters of the certification version prefer it?
o: Outside review confirms practices are real, so the shield rewards actual safety
Certified developers also gain immunity from criminal prosecution for harms their AI causes
Certified models are exempt from having to comply with any state or federal AI law
Auditors pay victims directly whenever a certified model causes harm
ow: The proposals discussed here concern civil liability; criminal immunity is not part of them.
Certification is meant to show a developer meets standards; it grants no exemption from other laws.
Auditors check practices; compensation still comes from developers or insurers.
keys: independent review checks the practices are real
the shield rewards real safety practice over a self-written document
items.x: Dean Ball, who favors the certification version, argues published safety frameworks are only starting points, and audits would test whether labs follow them. Gabriel Weil said Illinois SB 3444, which shields developers that publish a safety plan, offers 'near total protection from liability' for 'a very weak requirement'. California's SB 813 (signed Sept. 9, 2026) creates a framework for independent verification organizations to assess AI models for compliance with state law, but in its final form a passed audit is only 'relevant to, but not conclusive of' a lawsuit, so it is not a full safe harbor.

items.p: Illinois SB 3444 (2026), backed by OpenAI, would shield frontier developers that publish a safety plan from liability for critical harms (death or serious injury to 100+ people, or over $1 billion in property damage) unless they acted intentionally or recklessly. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: it trades near-total immunity for a weak, unenforced requirement (Gabriel Weil called it 'pretty indefensible'); requiring intent or recklessness is far stricter than usual for dangerous activities, where fault normally doesn't matter, and intent is hard to prove with AI (Anat Lior); Anthropic opposed it, saying good legislation shouldn't provide a 'get-out-of-jail-free card'.
keys: near-total immunity in exchange for a weak, unenforced requirement
requiring intent or recklessness is far stricter than usual for dangerous activities
intent is hard to prove with AI
Anthropic opposed it as a get-out-of-jail-free card
items.x: 'Reckless' means consciously ignoring a known, serious risk; 'intentional' means meaning to cause harm. So ordinary carelessness, which negligence would cover, would no longer create liability for these harms. Experts told Fortune in April 2026 the bill was unlikely to pass; Anthropic backed a competing Illinois bill (SB 3261).

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raised to Illinois SB 3444's liability shield for frontier developers?
o: It grants near-total immunity in return for a safety plan no one enforces
It makes developers pay for catastrophic harms even when they took every precaution
It requires developers to buy insurance that no insurer currently sells
It lets rival labs agree to delay releases without antitrust review
ow: That describes strict liability, the opposite of a shield.
SB 3444 has no insurance requirement.
That describes an antitrust safe harbor such as the CATS Act.

items.p: Besides liability shields for developers, some propose an AI 'safe harbor' for safety research. Whom would it protect, and from what?
o: Independent safety researchers, from account bans or legal action under terms of service
AI developers, from lawsuits over harms caused by the people who use their models
Lab employees, from losing their vested equity when they report dangers
Small startups, from state AI laws written with only large labs in mind
ow: That would be a developer liability shield, which this proposal is not.
That is the goal of whistleblower protections.
That concerns thresholds and preemption, a separate debate.
keys: protects independent safety researchers or red-teamers
from account suspensions or legal reprisal under terms of service
items.x: The proposal comes from Shayne Longpre and co-authors (2024), who argue that terms of service discourage good-faith safety research and that company-run researcher access programs lack independence. They ask major developers to commit to legal and technical protections for public-interest evaluation, so that terms of service don't deter outside testing.

items.p: What gap do supporters say AI whistleblower protections close?
items.answer: Lab employees are often the first to see dangerous capabilities, skipped safety tests or misleading public statements, but contracts and fear of retaliation can keep them quiet. Protection makes it safer to tell regulators or Congress, giving government a window into labs without building a large new agency.
keys: insiders see problems first
contracts or retaliation keep them silent
gives government visibility into labs
items.x: In May 2024, Vox reported that OpenAI's exit paperwork tied departing employees' vested equity to signing a non-disparagement clause; OpenAI then removed the clause and released former employees from it. California's SB 53 has protected covered frontier-lab employees who report catastrophic risks since Jan. 1, 2026.

choice.p: What gap do supporters say AI whistleblower protections close?
o: Insiders who see dangers first can be silenced by contracts or fear of retaliation
Developers can't pay for huge harms, which leaves their victims uncompensated
Rival labs can't legally agree to slow down together, even for safety
Courts lack the technical experts needed to judge AI lawsuits fairly
ow: That is the gap insurance mandates target.
That is the gap an antitrust safe harbor targets.
Court expertise is a real issue, but whistleblower laws don't address it.

items.p: Besides reports of federal-law violations, the AI Whistleblower Protection Act (S. 1792) protects reports that an employer failed to respond appropriately to a 'substantial and specific danger' from AI. Why do supporters say protection beyond illegal conduct matters?
items.answer: Few laws specifically regulate AI risks, so many of the most serious warnings (such as dangerous capabilities or skipped safety testing) may involve no legal violation. Protections limited to illegal activity would leave insiders who raise them exposed.
keys: few AI-specific laws exist
serious dangers may involve no legal violation
protections limited to illegal activity would leave these insiders exposed
items.x: Current and former OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Anthropic employees made this case in their June 2024 'Right to Warn' letter, saying ordinary protections 'focus on illegal activity'. Sen. Chuck Grassley introduced S. 1792 on May 15, 2025, with a House companion (H.R. 3460) from Reps. Jay Obernolte and Ted Lieu. As of October 2026 both bills remain in committee.

choice.p: Why do supporters say AI whistleblower laws should protect reports of serious dangers, beyond reports of illegal conduct?
o: Few AI-specific laws exist, so many serious dangers break no law
Danger reports are easier for regulators to verify than legal violations
Federal law otherwise bars employees from reporting legal violations to Congress
It lets labs sue employees whose danger reports turn out to be false
ow: Supporters argue that many serious dangers break no law; ease of verification isn't their point.
No federal law bars such reports; the gap is that many AI dangers break no law.
The bill protects people who report; it creates no right to sue them.

items.p: Vox reported in 2024 that OpenAI's exit paperwork tied departing employees' vested equity to a non-disparagement clause. What does the AI Whistleblower Protection Act (S. 1792) say about contracts that would limit its protections?
o: No contract or job condition, even an arbitration deal, can waive them
Labs must publish every employment and exit agreement they ask workers to sign
Departing employees may sell their vested equity before they leave
Non-compete clauses at AI companies become unenforceable
ow: The bill has no requirement to publish agreements.
The bill provides retaliation remedies; it has no equity-sale provision.
Non-competes are a separate employment-law issue the bill does not address.
keys: contracts or conditions of employment cannot waive or alter its rights and remedies
includes agreements requiring arbitration before seeking relief
items.x: The rights 'may not be waived or altered' by any contract or condition of employment. A worker who faces retaliation files with the Labor Department, can go to federal court with a jury if there's no decision within 180 days, and can win reinstatement and double back pay. The AI Whistleblower Initiative notes the bill does not bar agreements that deter reporting in the first place.

items.p: The federal AI Whistleblower Protection Act would protect AI workers who report dangers or legal violations to regulators or Congress. Name two gaps or limits critics point out.
items.answer: Examples: staff at outside evaluation organizations may not count as covered workers; unvested equity isn't clearly covered in remedies; there are no civil penalties for retaliation; its violation definition covers federal law only, leaving reports about state AI laws unprotected; it is silent on when going public is protected; danger reports must also show a 'failure to appropriately respond'.
keys: outside evaluators may be excluded
unvested equity not clearly covered
no civil penalties for retaliation
covers only federal-law violations
silent on going public
items.x: These come from a July 2026 analysis by the AI Whistleblower Initiative and CARMA, which recommends fixes. The bill's backing crosses party lines: Senate cosponsors at introduction included Democrats Chris Coons, Amy Klobuchar and Brian Schatz and Republicans Marsha Blackburn and Josh Hawley.

choice.p: Which of these is a gap critics have identified in the federal AI Whistleblower Protection Act?
o: Staff at outside evaluation firms may not count as covered workers
It protects only reports of illegal conduct, leaving danger reports out
It lets labs enforce NDAs against workers who talk to Congress
It requires whistleblowers to go public before reporting to regulators
ow: The bill also covers reports about substantial and specific dangers.
The bill says no contract can waive its rights and remedies.
The bill protects reports to regulators and Congress; it requires no public disclosure.

items.p: Antitrust law generally bars competitors from agreeing to limit their products. Why do some people propose an antitrust safe harbor for AI safety coordination?
items.answer: So labs can share security threat information and agree to slow or delay training or releases for safety without risking an illegal-collusion lawsuit. Without it, no lab wants to slow down alone, and a joint slowdown could be treated as a cartel.
keys: lets labs share safety or security threat information
lets labs agree to slow or delay for safety
without it, joint slowdowns could count as illegal collusion
no lab wants to slow down alone
items.x: Supporters describe a collective-action problem: each lab may prefer that everyone slow down, but none will slow down alone. In September 2026, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for industry-wide coordination to 'pace the frontier' and suggested some of it might need waivers of antitrust restrictions.

choice.p: Why do some people propose an antitrust safe harbor for AI safety coordination?
o: So labs can share threat data and slow releases without collusion suits
So labs can pool customer data to train safer models without facing privacy suits
So the government can force rival labs to merge into one national AI project
So labs can set common prices to help fund the cost of their safety research
ow: Proposals cover security-risk information; pooling customer data raises separate privacy issues.
A safe harbor permits voluntary coordination; it forces nothing.
Price-fixing stays illegal under proposals such as the CATS Act.

items.p: Under current US antitrust law, which kind of AI safety cooperation among rival labs carries the most legal risk?
o: A standalone agreement to pause or slow AI development
Sharing information about cybersecurity threats
Jointly publishing best practices for alignment research
One lab deciding on its own to delay a release
ow: A September 2026 CRS analysis found cybersecurity information sharing unlikely to raise significant concerns.
Shared best practices would likely be judged under the more forgiving 'rule of reason'.
Section 1 of the Sherman Act covers only agreements between separate firms; a solo decision is no agreement.
keys: a standalone pause or slowdown agreement
output limits can be per se illegal
items.x: Agreements among competitors to limit output can be 'per se' illegal, meaning courts condemn them without weighing their effects. Most other collaboration gets the 'rule of reason', which weighs harms against benefits. CRS notes a pause tied to a broader safety-evaluation regime might fare better than a bare one.

items.p: The CATS Act (H.R. 9914 / S. 5105, July 2026) would let AI labs agree to delay or limit releases to reduce defined security risks. What must labs do before starting such an agreement?
o: Notify DOJ's Antitrust Division in writing, describing the specific risk
Get prior approval from the competition bureau of the Federal Trade Commission
Publish the agreement's full terms in the Federal Register for public comment
Get a federal court order confirming that the agreement is lawful
ow: The bill gives the FTC no approval role.
The bill requires notice to DOJ; it has no Federal Register step.
The bill requires notice only; no court approval comes first.
keys: prior written notice to DOJ's Antitrust Division
the notice details the specific security risk
items.x: Covered risks include theft or weaponization of models by adversary nations, major help with chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear or cyber weapons, loss of human control over AI, and dangerous autonomous self-improvement. The bill says its information-sharing exemption does not permit price-fixing, market allocation or boycotts, and the Attorney General can seek a court order against coordination likely to increase overall risk.

items.p: The CATS Act would give AI labs an antitrust safe harbor to coordinate on security risks, including agreeing to delay releases. Name two objections critics raise to safe harbors like this.
items.answer: Examples: safety standards set by a few dominant labs could shore up their market position (Daniel Hanley and Arnav Rao, Open Markets Institute); no exemption is needed, since existing law allows much safety collaboration (American Action Forum); labs could use safety as a pretext for a pause that serves commercial goals; a US pause could hand Chinese firms an edge.
keys: could entrench dominant labs
unnecessary: existing law allows much safety collaboration
safety could be a pretext for commercial goals
a US pause could give Chinese firms an edge
items.x: A September 2026 CRS analysis notes both the pretext concern and officials' worry about China. Hanley and Rao propose a broadly representative, government-supervised standards body instead, with open-source developers, customers and governments at the table. Joel Thayer of the America First Policy Institute said he is skeptical of giving labs 'carte blanche control' over their data-sharing arrangements.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to an antitrust safe harbor for AI safety coordination?
o: Standards set by a few dominant labs could entrench their position
It makes labs pay for harms even when they took every reasonable precaution
It leaves insiders who report dangers open to retaliation
It forces labs to buy liability insurance before each new model release
ow: That is a feature of strict liability.
That is the gap whistleblower protections target.
The CATS Act concerns coordination and contains no insurance requirement.

items.p: On Sept. 18, 2026, paying subscribers filed a class action against Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceX AI and Google DeepMind. What did they allege?
o: That the labs illegally agreed to slow AI development, degrading what customers buy
That the labs fixed the subscription prices they charge for their chatbots
That the labs' safety testing was negligent and caused harm to users
That the labs shared their users' personal data with each other without consent
ow: The claim concerns slowing development, a restraint on output; it does not allege price-fixing.
The suit is an antitrust claim; it does not allege negligent testing.
The suit concerns an alleged slowdown agreement; it does not allege data sharing.
keys: an illegal agreement to slow AI development
reduced the quality of what subscribers pay for
items.x: The suit invokes Section 1 of the Sherman Act (the federal ban on agreements that restrain trade) and traces the alleged agreement to Dario Amodei's Sept. 12, 2026 essay calling on labs to 'pace the frontier', which Elon Musk, Sam Altman and Demis Hassabis publicly praised. These are allegations only; the American Action Forum notes that Anthropic committed on its own only to embedding outside evaluators.

items.p: Some reformers want frontier labs legally bound to a public mission through nonprofit control, independent trusts or mission-bound boards, with state attorneys general enforcing it. What failure are these structures meant to prevent?
items.answer: If a lab's board answers only to investors, commercial pressure wins close calls about training, releasing and using the most capable systems. Mission-locked governance puts a body with no stake in profits between the lab and that pressure, and attorney general oversight adds outside enforcement.
keys: boards answerable only to investors let profit win close safety calls
a body with no profit stake checks those decisions
attorneys general enforce the mission from outside
items.x: This tool works through corporate and charity law, since whoever controls a frontier lab decides how its systems are trained and released. A public benefit corporation (PBC) is a for-profit company whose charter requires its board to weigh a stated public mission alongside profits.

choice.p: What failure are mission-locked lab governance structures, such as nonprofit control or independent trusts, meant to prevent?
o: Investor-only boards letting commercial pressure win close safety calls
Employees leaking model weights to foreign governments for money
Rival labs colluding to raise the prices they charge customers
Regulators lacking the technical expertise to evaluate models
ow: Weight security is a separate problem handled by security standards.
Collusion is an antitrust problem; these structures concern who controls a single lab.
Regulatory capacity is a separate issue; these structures work inside the company.

items.p: Under OpenAI's October 2025 agreement with California's attorney general, what authority does the nonprofit's Safety and Security Committee hold?
o: Require safety measures, up to halting a release, even if risk thresholds allow it
Fire OpenAI's chief executive at any time without a vote of the full nonprofit board
Hold a majority of the voting shares in OpenAI's for-profit company
Impose fines on OpenAI when it breaks its public safety commitments
ow: Its authority is limited to safety and security decisions about models and systems.
Control runs through the nonprofit's special Class N shares; the committee itself holds no shares.
It can require mitigations; fines are a government power.
keys: can require mitigation measures
up to halting a model release
even when risk thresholds would permit release
items.x: The committee belongs to the nonprofit, and its chair (Zico Kolter) sits on the nonprofit board only. The nonprofit appoints and can remove the for-profit PBC's directors, and must give the attorney general at least 21 days' notice before charter changes that would remove that power.

items.p: Anthropic uses a different structure, the Long-Term Benefit Trust. What power does the trust hold?
o: Trustees with no financial stake elect up to a majority of the board
It must sign off on every Anthropic model before that model can be released
It owns a majority of Anthropic's stock through its special share class
It appoints Anthropic's chief executive directly and can remove them at will
ow: The trust works through board elections; it has no per-release approval right.
The trust holds a special class of stock (Class T) for electing directors, with no majority ownership.
The board chooses the CEO; the trust elects part of the board.
keys: trustees with no financial stake in the company
elect a growing share of the board, eventually a majority
items.x: The trust holds special Class T stock, and Anthropic said in 2023 the trust would elect a board majority within four years. Stockholders can still change the trust's powers without trustee consent if large supermajorities agree, a 'failsafe' Anthropic built in.

items.p: OpenAI's 2025 restructuring kept a nonprofit in control of its for-profit company, under state attorney general oversight. Name two objections critics raise to relying on this kind of lab governance.
items.answer: Examples: paper commitments may not change behavior (Public Citizen's Robert Weissman said OpenAI has consistently put the for-profit's goals first); mission boards can fold under pressure, as when OpenAI's board fired its CEO in November 2023 and reversed within days; such structures bind only labs that choose them, and owners can loosen them later.
keys: paper commitments may not change behavior
mission bodies can fold under investor or employee pressure
binds only labs that opt in, and owners can loosen it
items.x: On Nov. 17, 2023, OpenAI's nonprofit board removed Sam Altman; after 745 of its 770 employees signed a letter threatening to quit, he was back as CEO within days. Gabriel Weil cites that episode as a sign that internal governance can't be fully relied on. In May 2026, a jury rejected Elon Musk's suit over OpenAI's shift toward a for-profit structure, finding he had brought it too late.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to relying on nonprofit or trust control to keep AI labs safe?
o: Mission boards can fold under pressure from investors and staff
It makes labs pay for harms even when they took every precaution
It lets rival labs coordinate releases without antitrust review
It requires labs to buy catastrophe insurance before going public
ow: That describes strict liability.
That describes an antitrust safe harbor.
Governance structures change who controls a lab; insurance is a separate tool.

items.p: Match each liability or lab-governance tool to the failure it mainly targets.
pairs: Duty of care
Labs skip precautions because much of the harm would fall on others
Mandatory insurance
A developer can't pay for a huge harm, so victims go uncompensated
Liability safe harbor
Developers face uncertain lawsuit risk and no reward for verified safety practices
Whistleblower protections
Insiders who see dangers stay silent out of fear of retaliation
Antitrust safe harbor
No lab will slow down alone, and a joint slowdown could count as a cartel
Mission-locked governance
Boards answerable only to investors let profit win close safety calls
items.x: Strict liability targets the same underinvestment in safety as a duty of care but reaches further: the developer pays even when it took every known precaution.

items.p: A small AI startup's model helps cause a $2 billion cyberattack. A court finds the startup liable, but it has only $50 million in assets. Which tool most directly addresses this gap?
o: Mandatory insurance or financial assurance
Strict liability for AI developers
A statutory duty of care
An antitrust safe harbor for safety coordination
ow: Strict liability makes it easier to hold the startup liable, but it still can't pay what it owes.
A duty of care creates liability, which already exists here; the problem is collecting.
Coordination among labs does nothing for victims who can't collect damages.
keys: mandatory liability insurance or financial assurance
solves the judgment-proof problem
items.x: A defendant that can't pay is 'judgment-proof'. Required coverage means a solvent insurer stands behind the developer, and premiums give the developer a reason to reduce risk in advance.

items.p: A lab followed every safety practice known in the industry, yet its model still gave crucial help in a serious attack. Under which liability rule could victims most easily recover from the lab?
o: Strict liability
A negligence-based duty of care
A safe harbor for publishing a safety plan
A requirement to carry liability insurance
ow: Negligence requires showing the lab failed to take reasonable care, which is hard when it followed every known practice.
A safe harbor would shield the lab from these suits.
Insurance pays claims the lab is liable for; it doesn't decide whether the lab is liable.
keys: strict liability
liable without proof of carelessness
items.x: Strict liability asks whether the system caused the harm, without asking whether the lab was careless. Supporters such as Gabriel Weil say this suits risks no one yet knows how to prevent.

items.p: Match each legal term to its plain-English meaning.
pairs: Negligence
Liability for failing to take the care a reasonable person would
Strict liability
Liability for harm caused, even after taking every precaution
Punitive damages
Extra damages beyond the victim's losses, meant to punish or deter
Safe harbor
Conditions that, if met, protect you from a penalty or lawsuit
Judgment-proof
Unable to pay what a court awards
Per se illegal
Unlawful without courts weighing the conduct's effects
items.x: Most tools in this unit adjust one of these levers: whether a developer pays without fault (strict liability versus negligence), how much (punitive damages), whether it can pay (insurance), and when it is excused (safe harbors).

units.title: Compute, chips and security
units.desc: Tools that control who gets advanced chips and compute, protect frontier models from theft, govern open release, and screen DNA orders as a biosecurity chokepoint.

items.p: Export controls require licenses to sell advanced AI chips and chipmaking tools to China and other countries of concern. How do supporters say this reduces risk from advanced AI?
items.answer: Frontier AI takes huge numbers of advanced chips, and a few U.S. and allied firms control their supply. Restricting that supply slows rivals' frontier development and limits the compute their militaries and labs can use, which supporters say keeps the U.S. and its allies in the lead.
keys: frontier AI needs huge numbers of advanced chips
a few U.S. and allied firms control supply, a chokepoint
slows rivals' frontier development
keeps the U.S. and allies ahead and limits adversary militaries
items.x: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei argued in January 2025 that the controls keep 'democratic nations at the forefront of AI development.' The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) writes the rules under the Export Control Reform Act of 2018. The theory assumes controls hold up against smuggling and cloud rental, and that China can't quickly build substitutes.

choice.p: How do supporters say chip export controls reduce risk from advanced AI?
o: Limiting sales of chips a few U.S. and allied firms control slows rivals and keeps a lead
Tracking where each chip is located lets officials catch chips smuggled to banned buyers
Checking who rents cloud compute lets the government see who is training very large models
Requiring strong security at data centers keeps rivals from stealing trained frontier models
ow: That describes chip location verification, a tool for enforcing export controls after chips are sold.
That describes cloud know-your-customer rules, which cover renting chips remotely.
That describes data center and weight security, which protect models that are already trained.

items.p: As introduced in December 2025, what would the AI OVERWATCH Act (H.R. 6875) add to the rules for selling advanced AI chips to China and other countries of concern?
o: A license requirement in law, plus 30 days' notice to Congress, which could block a license
A requirement that exported chips carry location verification, so that smuggled chips can be detected and reported to Commerce
A requirement that cloud providers verify the identity of foreign customers who rent advanced chips remotely
A permanent ban on all advanced chip sales to China, with no licenses allowed under any conditions
ow: That is the Chip Security Act, a separate bill aimed at smuggling.
That is the cloud know-your-customer idea; the Remote Access Security Act covers remote access.
The bill keeps licensing and adds congressional review, though it would pause approvals until the administration delivers a required strategy.
keys: license requirement written into statute
Congress gets at least 30 days' notice before a license is approved
Congress can block a license by joint resolution
items.x: Today the rules are Commerce Department regulations, so an administration can loosen them, as Commerce did for H200 chips in January 2026. In September 2026 five tech industry groups, including ITI, objected that the bill would freeze chip controls in statute for at least 18 months, 'an eternity in the fast-moving AI sector.' In July 2026 a version was added to the Senate's manager's package of amendments to its FY27 defense bill (NDAA).

items.p: Some experts want export controls to focus more on chipmaking equipment, and on getting allies such as the Netherlands and Japan to match U.S. rules. What gap does this target?
o: China making its own advanced chips, using tools that allied firms can still sell
Chinese firms renting U.S. chips through cloud data centers in third countries, where the chips were shipped legally
Licensed chips that are later smuggled to places their licenses don't allow
Hackers stealing the trained weights of frontier models from U.S. labs
ow: That is the cloud-rental gap, which know-your-customer and remote-access rules target.
That is the smuggling gap, which chip location verification targets.
That is the theft risk that model weight security standards target.
keys: limits China's own production of advanced chips
chipmaking depends on foreign equipment such as Dutch lithography machines
allied firms can sell tools U.S. firms can't, so allies must match
items.x: In November 2025 House testimony, Dean Ball argued the U.S. had controlled chips but not 'the machines that make the machines.' He said China depends on lithography machines from the Dutch firm ASML for its advanced AI chips, and that Japanese toolmakers could sell to China while U.S. firms were largely barred. The MATCH Act aims at these gaps between U.S. and allied rules.

items.p: Chip export controls: limits on selling advanced AI chips and chipmaking tools to China and other countries of concern. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: they push China to make its own chips faster (like Huawei's), so the lead may shrink; they cost U.S. chipmakers market share and revenue; smuggling and cloud rental undercut them; treating chips as a race asset can make U.S.-China safety talks harder.
keys: speeds up Chinese domestic substitutes
costs U.S. companies market share
undercut by smuggling or cloud access
makes cooperation or agreements harder
items.x: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang called the controls 'a failure' in May 2025, saying they cut Nvidia's China market share from about 95% to 50% and pushed China to make its own chips faster. How fast Chinese substitutes are catching up is disputed. Supporters such as Anthropic's Dario Amodei reply that well-enforced controls are the only thing that can stop China from getting millions of advanced chips.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to chip export controls?
o: They push China to build its own chips, so the U.S. lead may shrink over time
Kill switches built into chips would give hackers a single point of failure
Fine-tuning can strip safeguards from a model once its weights are published
Publishing safety frameworks would reveal trade secrets to foreign rivals
ow: That objection targets on-chip remote-disable proposals; export controls limit sales and put nothing inside chips.
That is an argument made by supporters of open-weight limits, about a different tool.
That is an objection to transparency rules for AI developers, which export controls don't involve.

items.p: In January 2026, how did the Commerce Department change its rules for exporting Nvidia H200 chips to China?
o: It moved license reviews from presumed denial to case-by-case, if conditions such as U.S. lab testing are met
It banned all H200 sales to China, closing a loophole that had let Chinese firms buy older Nvidia chips freely
It allowed sales of Nvidia's newest Blackwell chips to approved Chinese buyers
It required every exported H200 to carry location verification before shipping
ow: The rule loosened policy; before it, such licenses were presumed denied.
Blackwell chips exceed the rule's performance limits, so their licenses stay presumed denied.
Location verification is in the Chip Security Act, which had not become law.
keys: case-by-case license review
replaced a presumption of denial
conditions such as independent third-party testing in the U.S. before export
items.x: The change followed President Trump's December 2025 announcement that the government would get a 25% cut of H200 sales. A January 14, 2026 proclamation set a 25% tariff on certain advanced chips imported into the U.S., which Covington notes would presumably apply to foreign-made chips brought in for the required U.S. testing. Reuters reported that Beijing told its tech firms not to buy the chips unless absolutely necessary.

items.p: Some proposals add location verification to AI chips. What is it meant to accomplish?
items.answer: In the near term, catching smuggling and diversion of export-controlled chips, which current enforcement misses. In the longer run, a technical base for verifying compliance with international compute limits without trusting the other side.
keys: catch smuggling or diversion of controlled chips
current enforcement misses much diversion
could verify international compute agreements
items.x: Narrow versions only estimate roughly which country a chip is in, using signal delays; broader proposals would also verify what chips are used for.

choice.p: What are chip location verification requirements meant to accomplish?
o: Catch chip smuggling now, and later help verify international compute limits
