Let the government switch off any chip remotely as soon as it is misused anywhere in the world
Show regulators which cloud customers are renting chips to train the largest AI models
Stop hackers and insiders from copying model weights out of data centers
ow: Remote disable is a stronger, more opposed proposal; location checks only report roughly where a chip is.
That is the job of cloud know-your-customer rules.
That is the job of model weight and data center security standards.

items.p: On-chip proposals for AI chips range from location verification to much stronger mechanisms. What separates location verification from the strongest versions?
o: Location checks report roughly where a chip is; strong versions could stop it working
Location checks apply only to chips sold in the U.S.; the strong versions also cover exported chips
Location checks are voluntary for chipmakers; the strong versions are already required by law
Location checks stop smuggling before it happens; the strong versions only detect it afterward
ow: The Chip Security Act would apply location checks to export-controlled chips.
Neither is law; the Chip Security Act would require location checks and only study stronger mechanisms.
Location checks detect diversion only after it happens (CSET); the strong versions could then stop a diverted chip from working.
keys: location verification only reports approximate location
strong versions can disable a chip or require license renewal
that creates a remote off switch, the most opposed feature
items.x: Nvidia's chief security officer wrote in August 2025 that its chips 'do not and should not have kill switches and backdoors,' arguing they create single points of failure for hackers. The Chip Security Act would require location verification and have Commerce assess whether further mechanisms should be added.

items.p: The Chip Security Act would require export-controlled AI chips to carry location verification. Name two objections or limits that critics raise about location verification and similar on-chip mechanisms.
items.answer: Examples: it places chips only to about the country level and can't see a chip handed to a different user at the same site (CSET); well-funded adversaries may spoof it; it catches diversion only after the fact; tracking and costly, unproven features could erode global trust in U.S. chips (SIA, ITI); built-in controls create hacking and abuse risks (Nvidia).
keys: only country-level accuracy; misses a new user at the same site
well-resourced adversaries can spoof it
detects diversion only after it happens
cost, unproven tech or tracking could erode trust in U.S. chips
built-in controls create hacking or government-abuse risks
items.x: CSET's September 2026 study still judged ping-based checks, with physical inspections to follow up leads, the most robust and feasible approach, at roughly $2.6 million to $72 million a year. The Semiconductor Industry Association and a coalition of tech groups including ITI opposed the bill, while six shipment-tracking companies backed it.

choice.p: Which of these is a limit critics point to in chip location verification?
o: It places chips only to about the country level, so it misses a new user at the same site
It depends on customers telling the truth about who they are and where they operate
It would block advanced chip sales to close allies such as Japan and the Netherlands
It works only on old chips, since it can't be built into new chip designs
ow: That is the U.S. Chamber's objection to cloud know-your-customer rules; location checks rely on network signal timing.
The bill tracks where exported chips go; it doesn't bar sales to allies.
It's closer to the reverse: CSET notes hardware versions can't be added to chips already in service.

items.p: As of mid-October 2026, where did the Chip Security Act (H.R. 3447) stand?
o: Approved 42-0 by the House Foreign Affairs Committee in March 2026, and not yet law
Signed into law in 2025 as part of the White House AI Action Plan
Withdrawn after Nvidia said its chips would never include tracking
Passed by the full House 369-22 in January 2026 and sent to the Senate
ow: The bill was introduced in May 2025 and had not been enacted.
Nvidia opposed kill switches, but the bill kept moving; it was not withdrawn.
That vote was on the Remote Access Security Act, a different chip bill.
keys: approved 42-0 by House Foreign Affairs, March 2026
not enacted
proposed for the Senate's FY27 NDAA in a manager's package
items.x: In July 2026 its text was added, with AI OVERWATCH and the MATCH Act, to a manager's package of amendments for the Senate's FY27 defense bill (NDAA), which had not passed the Senate as of mid-October. In September 2026 five tech industry groups, including ITI, urged NDAA negotiators to drop all three. As introduced, the bill gives Commerce 180 days after enactment to require location verification.

items.p: Why do proposals require cloud providers that rent out AI chips to know their customers?
items.answer: Export controls restrict sales of advanced chips, but companies in restricted countries can rent the same chips through cloud data centers. Know-your-customer rules aim to let the government see who is training very large models and deny service to adversaries.
keys: closes the cloud-rental gap in export controls
lets government see who trains very large models
can deny service to adversaries
items.x: Commerce proposed a customer identification rule for cloud (infrastructure-as-a-service) providers in January 2024, which would also have required reports on foreign customers whose transactions could help train large AI models. Supporters Janet Egan and Lennart Heim describe compute as 'emerging as a node for oversight' of frontier AI.

choice.p: Why do proposals require cloud providers that rent out AI chips to know their customers?
o: Restricted firms can rent controlled chips through the cloud, so providers check who rents
Cloud data centers are the easiest place for hackers to steal trained model weights
Chips installed in cloud data centers are often smuggled abroad later without anyone noticing
Cloud providers run most open-weight models, so tracking renters stops their spread
ow: That is the concern behind data center and model weight security standards.
Smuggling is what chip location verification targets.
KYC is about who rents compute for training; open-weight policy is a separate debate.

items.p: The Remote Access Security Act (H.R. 2683) takes a different route from a cloud know-your-customer rule. What does it do?
o: Lets Commerce control foreign persons' remote access to controlled items, such as AI chips
Requires every cloud provider to verify all customers' identities and report large training runs
Requires chips sold abroad to report their location to Commerce over the network
Bars U.S. cloud companies from building AI data centers in countries of concern
ow: That is the broader customer identification approach, as in Commerce's 2024 proposed rule.
That is the Chip Security Act's location verification requirement.
The bill regulates access to controlled items; it doesn't ban building data centers.
keys: applies export controls to remote access, including through the cloud
foreign persons' access to controlled items can need a license
lets Commerce (BIS) license and penalize remote access
items.x: The House passed it 369-22 on January 12, 2026, and it went to the Senate Banking Committee. CRS describes remote access as access 'through a network connection, including the internet or a cloud computing service.' The passed text reaches any item under U.S. export jurisdiction, which IAPS notes could include AI models offered as software services.

items.p: Besides helping enforce export controls, what could know-your-customer rules for large cloud compute customers give the government?
o: Visibility into frontier AI work, to spot sudden capability jumps
Authority to approve or reject each new frontier AI model before the developer can release it publicly
A share of the revenue cloud providers earn from their foreign AI customers
A government registry of where every exported AI chip is physically located
ow: That would be a licensing regime for models; KYC covers who rents compute.
Revenue cuts came up for H200 sales to China; this proposal includes none.
Tracking chip locations is the job of location verification.
keys: visibility into who is doing frontier-scale training
flag sudden or risky capability jumps
build government capacity to regulate AI
items.x: Janet Egan and Lennart Heim, who proposed such rules for customers above a compute threshold, argue a threshold that is updated over time can capture high-risk frontier work without burdening ordinary cloud customers, and that controlling access to compute is more precise than restricting chip purchases, since access can be adjusted or suspended at any time.

items.p: Cloud know-your-customer rules: providers that rent out AI chips would verify customers' identities and report foreign customers or very large training runs. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: bad actors can fake or conceal their identities, so checks rely on them telling the truth (U.S. Chamber of Commerce); compliance is costly, especially for small businesses; strict rules could hand business to foreign cloud providers; clashes with foreign privacy rules; a broad remote-access definition could let Commerce control who uses U.S. AI models (a concern IAPS raises).
keys: easy to evade with false or concealed identities
costly compliance, especially for small firms
pushes customers to non-U.S. providers or hurts competitiveness
privacy concerns or conflicts with foreign privacy law
could give government broad control over access to AI services
items.x: The Chamber's 2024 comments said the proposed program 'depends on malicious cyber actors providing truthful information' about themselves. IAPS analyst Cassia King warned that the House remote-access bill's broad definition appears to reach software services, which could in effect let Commerce control access to AI models.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to cloud know-your-customer rules?
o: Bad actors can fake or conceal their identities, so the checks are easy to evade
Location checks can place a chip only to within roughly one country
Reaching the top security level may take years and need national security help
A model's weights can't be recalled once they have been posted online
ow: That is a limit of chip location verification.
That is a difficulty with mandatory model weight security levels.
That is part of the case for limits on open-weight release.

items.p: Why do proposals to prevent theft of frontier models attach security requirements to AI data centers in particular?
items.answer: Frontier model weights and secrets are stored and used in data centers, so a breach there could undo other safeguards. Builders also need things government controls, such as grid connections, land and permits, so security can be made a condition of those benefits. Supporters say this fixes a market failure: labs racing each other underinvest in security.
keys: weights and secrets are stored and used there
a breach there undoes other safeguards
builders need grid power, land or permits from government
security can be made a condition of those benefits
racing labs underinvest in security on their own
items.x: IFP's 2025 'Compute in America' playbook proposed tying federal energy and permitting help, including sites on federal land, to security requirements, arguing that labs that spend enough to stop Chinese state hackers risk falling behind rivals. The approach assumes standards can reach nation-state level in time and that builders don't move abroad.

choice.p: Why do proposals to prevent theft of frontier models attach security requirements to AI data centers in particular?
o: Model weights sit there, and builders need grid power, land and permits, giving leverage
Data centers store users' chat histories, so the rules mainly protect consumer privacy
Data centers are where export-controlled chips are most often smuggled out of the country
Data centers are where cloud customers' identities are checked before they can rent chips
ow: Privacy laws apply too, but these proposals aim to stop rival states stealing or sabotaging frontier models.
Smuggling is the target of chip location verification.
Checking renters is the job of cloud know-your-customer rules.

items.p: One proposal would give large AI data centers a fast lane for grid hookups if they agree to cut power use when the grid is strained and accept binding security controls on their grid-facing systems. What risk is the security condition meant to address?
o: Hackers seizing a site's load controls to swing its power use and destabilize the grid
Spies or hackers stealing the frontier model weights stored on the data center's servers
Data center demand driving up electricity prices for households served by the same grid
Foreign-made chips with hidden backdoors being installed in the data center's server racks
ow: Weight theft is a real data center risk, but grid-facing controls protect the grid; weight security is a separate tool.
Prices are a cost-allocation question; these controls target attacks on the grid.
Chip supply-chain risks are a separate concern; these controls cover the systems that interact with the grid.
keys: attackers taking over a data center's load-management systems
sudden gigawatt-scale swings in power use
destabilizing the grid
items.x: This is the 'speed-for-security bargain' from IFP (the Institute for Progress), set out in a June 2026 piece by Ben Schifman. Tens of thousands of software-controlled GPUs can drop or resume gigawatt-scale load in a fraction of a second, and an attacker who took over a site's load management could use that to force damaging swings. IFP wants FERC to condition the fast lane on interim security controls, since enforceable standards from the grid reliability body NERC are unlikely before at least 2028. 'Curtailment' means the load agrees to cut its power use when the grid is strained.

items.p: In July 2026, NIST released a draft publication on AI data center security (SP 800-239). Which description of it is accurate?
o: Voluntary guidance that leaves physical and personnel security out of scope
A binding federal rule that every large U.S. data center must meet by January 2028
A requirement that new AI data centers on federal land reach RAND's top security level, SL5, before opening
An export rule that bars U.S. firms from building or operating AI data centers in China
ow: It is voluntary for private companies and sets no compliance deadline.
It is voluntary guidance and requires no particular security level.
It is a threat and security gap analysis; it sets no export rules.
keys: voluntary
covers the computing environment (access, compute, storage)
physical, personnel and supply-chain security are left to a separate effort
items.x: The draft answers the July 2025 AI Action Plan's call for standards for high-security AI data centers, and comments closed September 25, 2026. NIST says the excluded areas will be handled by a related initiative. The law firm Wiley expects it could later shape federal procurement requirements, as earlier NIST guidance has.

items.p: Security conditions on AI data centers: government sets security standards and ties them to grid access, land, permits or contracts. Name two limits or objections analysts raise.
items.answer: Examples: NIST's voluntary draft covers only the computing environment, leaving physical, personnel and supply-chain security for later; binding grid security standards for data centers are unlikely before at least 2028, so early conditions rely on interim controls (IFP's Ben Schifman); grid-based leverage misses builders who make their own power or build abroad; security adds cost and delay.
keys: voluntary or partial scope, such as the NIST draft's exclusions
binding grid security standards unlikely before 2028
leverage misses builders who make their own power or build abroad
adds cost and delay
items.x: RAND's threat model for the most capable state attackers includes human spying and physical operations as well as hacking, which is why gaps in physical and personnel security matter. IFP notes that slow grid hookups already push some builders to make their own power ('behind the meter') or look abroad.

choice.p: Which of these is a limit analysts raise about security conditions on AI data centers?
o: Binding grid security standards for data centers are unlikely before at least 2028
Location checks can't tell apart nearby data centers run by different companies
Customers can rent compute under false identities that providers fail to catch
Fine-tuning can strip the safeguards from a model whose weights are public
ow: That is a limit of chip location verification.
That is an objection to cloud know-your-customer rules.
That is the argument for limits on open-weight release.

items.p: Why do security proposals treat theft of a frontier model's weights as such a serious risk?
items.answer: Weights are the product of very costly training. Whoever steals them can run the model cheaply without the developer's safeguards or monitoring, and spread it. That hands a rival the payoff of the training, speeding up a race, and undoes other controls such as export controls or deployment limits.
keys: weights embody very costly training
a thief can run the model without safeguards or monitoring, and spread it
rivals skip costly training, speeding a race
undoes other controls (export controls, deployment limits)
items.x: RAND's 2024 report says that once attackers have the weights, abusing the model without restrictions is 'eminently feasible,' needing only computing power to run it. Its recommendations for labs include keeping all copies of weights on a few monitored systems and cutting the number of people with access.

choice.p: Why do security proposals treat theft of a frontier model's weights as such a serious risk?
o: A thief can run the model without safeguards and skip costly training, undoing other controls
Stolen weights would expose the private data and chat histories of everyone who has used the model
Stolen weights would let attackers take control of the lab's data centers
Weights hold the only record of a model's safety tests, which regulators rely on
ow: Weights are learned parameters; the main worry is a rival running the model itself.
Weights are a model file; stealing them doesn't give control of any facility.
Test records are separate documents; weights are what make the model run.

items.p: Security levels for AI model weights are defined by the attacker they can stop. Put these attackers in order, from the weakest a lab might defend against to the strongest.
items.x: This ladder follows RAND's 2024 report on securing model weights, whose levels SL1 to SL5 are defined by attackers like these, from amateur hackers at SL1 to the top-priority operations of the most capable states at SL5. RAND said achieving SL5 was not yet possible, that it would likely need help from the national security community, and that the needed measures could take significant time (for example, five years) to build.
items: Cybercrime groups and insiders at the lab
Routine operations by leading state-sponsored hacking groups
Top-priority operations by the world's most capable nation-states

items.p: How does California's SB 53 (2025) address model weight security for large frontier developers?
o: Their published safety framework must describe how they secure unreleased weights, with no set level
They must reach RAND's SL4 security level, checked by an auditor, before training any new frontier model
They must store weights only in state-certified data centers inside California
They must give a state agency a copy of their weights for safekeeping
ow: SB 53 requires disclosure of practices; it doesn't mandate any security level.
SB 53 has no rule about where data centers are located.
SB 53 doesn't require handing over weights.
keys: disclosure in the developer's published framework
cybersecurity practices for unreleased weights
against unauthorized modification or transfer
no minimum security level
items.x: SB 53, signed September 29, 2025, applies this to 'large' frontier developers (over $500 million in annual revenue) and covers unauthorized changes or transfers by insiders or outsiders. Proposals for mandatory security levels that rise with capability would go further, typically using RAND's levels as the benchmark.

items.p: Mandatory weight security levels: frontier developers would have to meet a minimum security level, such as RAND's SL4 or SL5, that rises with model capability. Name two objections or difficulties that have been raised.
items.answer: Examples: the top levels can't be reached soon, since RAND judged SL5 not yet possible and likely to need national security help; the highest levels require large sacrifices in productivity and convenience (RAND); securing a model adds little once its weights, or a comparable model's, are public.
keys: top levels not reachable soon, or take years
likely needs government or national security help
costly; sacrifices productivity and convenience
little value once comparable weights are public
items.x: RAND judged protecting internet-connected models from the most capable attackers 'currently not feasible.' Its answer to the timing problem is to start the harder measures now, since they may take years to build.

choice.p: Which of these is a difficulty raised about mandatory weight security levels?
o: The top levels can't be reached soon and would likely need help from national security agencies
Location checks can be fooled by well-funded adversaries who fake a chip's position
Export controls push China to build its own chips, shrinking the U.S. lead
Binding grid security standards for data centers are unlikely before at least 2028
ow: That is a limit of chip location verification.
That is an objection to chip export controls.
That is a timing problem for grid security standards for data centers.

items.p: Why do some safety advocates want limits on publishing the weights of the most capable models?
items.answer: Once weights are public, anyone can fine-tune the safeguards away, and the release can't be recalled. So if a model has dangerous capabilities, such as meaningful help with cyberattacks or bioweapons, open release hands them to everyone permanently.
keys: fine-tuning can strip safeguards
a release can't be recalled
dangerous capabilities become available to anyone, permanently
items.x: Elizabeth Seger and co-authors argued in 2023 that some highly capable models should not be open-sourced, at least at first. FAR.AI researchers showed in 2025 that fine-tuning, through open weights or closed fine-tuning services, can produce models that help with harmful requests. Capability-threshold proposals would restrict only models above a dangerous-capability line.

choice.p: Why do some safety advocates want limits on publishing the weights of the most capable models?
o: Fine-tuning can strip safeguards from published weights, and a release can't be recalled
Published weights reveal the private data that was used to train the model
Open models are always more capable than the closed models they compete with
Publishing weights lets anyone see which chips were used and evade export controls
ow: Weights are learned parameters; the worry is what the model can do once anyone can modify it.
Capability varies by model; the concern applies only to the most capable ones.
Export controls cover chips; the worry about weights is removing safeguards.

items.p: Two kinds of proposals would restrict open-weight models: capability-threshold limits and limits on Chinese open models. Would either one restrict a weak open-weight model made in China, and why?
o: Chinese-model limits would restrict it, since they turn on origin, not capability
Threshold limits would cover it, since they treat Chinese models as high-risk by default
Both would cover it, since both apply to open models above a size cutoff
Neither would cover it, since both turn on what a model can do
ow: Threshold proposals turn on dangerous capabilities, whatever country the model comes from.
Threshold proposals leave models below the capability line open, and a weak model stays below it.
Chinese-model limits target country of origin, whatever the model can do.
keys: Chinese-model limits would restrict it
they turn on country of origin, regardless of capability
threshold limits turn on capability, so a weak model falls outside them
items.x: After Moonshot AI posted Kimi K3's weights in July 2026, CFR's Chris McGuire said the administration's concern with Chinese open models is 'that they originate from China.' He proposed cutting all Chinese models, open or closed, off from U.S. businesses, cloud providers and chips, while leaving U.S. open models alone.

items.p: Limits on open-weight release: developers couldn't publish downloadable weights for models above a dangerous-capability threshold. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: evidence that open models add much risk beyond closed models and the internet is thin (NTIA); limits could entrench the few big closed developers; open models spread market power and help safety research; other countries' open models would fill the gap, pushing innovation offshore.
keys: thin evidence of extra risk
entrenches closed incumbents or reduces competition
open models decentralize power or help research
others' open models fill the gap
items.x: In July 2026, 25 companies including Nvidia, Microsoft, Meta, OpenAI and Google signed a letter urging Washington to avoid 'premature restrictions' on open-weight models, arguing a clampdown would push innovation offshore and hand the field to China. Supporters of limits reply that a threshold would restrict only the most capable models and leave the rest open.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to limits on open-weight release?
o: Evidence that open models add much risk beyond closed models and web search is thin
Fine-tuning can strip the safeguards from a model once its weights are published
Export controls push China to build its own chips, shrinking the U.S. lead
Identity checks on cloud customers can be evaded with false identities
ow: That is the main argument for limits, made by their supporters.
That is an objection to chip export controls.
That is an objection to cloud know-your-customer rules.

items.p: In its 2024 report on AI models with widely available weights, what did the Commerce Department's NTIA recommend?
o: No new restrictions for now, while the government monitors risks and stays ready to act
A ban on releasing any model trained with more than 10^26 operations
A Commerce Department license before any open-weight model above a size threshold is released
Barring U.S. companies from using open-weight models made in China
ow: NTIA found the evidence didn't justify restrictions and proposed no compute-based ban.
NTIA recommended monitoring risks, while keeping restrictions available as a later option.
That idea gained attention in 2026; NTIA's recommendation was to monitor risks.
keys: no new restrictions now, since evidence was insufficient
actively monitor risks
be prepared to act, keeping restrictions possible later
items.x: NTIA said current evidence was 'not sufficient to definitively determine' that restrictions were warranted, or that they would never be. The July 2025 AI Action Plan added a section titled 'Encourage Open-Source and Open-Weight AI.'

items.p: Why do biosecurity proposals focus on screening DNA synthesis orders, rather than only on AI models?
items.answer: Turning a pathogen design into a weapon still requires physical DNA, and DNA synthesis is a narrow industry. Screening orders and customers there is a chokepoint that works no matter which AI model produced the design, including openly released ones.
keys: designs still need physical DNA
synthesis is a concentrated chokepoint
works regardless of which model was used, including open-weight models
items.x: The researchers behind a 2025 Science study on screening describe DNA synthesis as 'a choke point' in AI-assisted protein engineering. Proposals pair checks on orders with checks that customers are legitimate.

choice.p: Why do biosecurity proposals focus on screening DNA synthesis orders, rather than only on AI models?
o: Designs need physical DNA from a narrow industry, so screening covers any model
AI models can't meaningfully help with biology, so rules on models would have no effect
DNA synthesis companies run most of the AI biology models, so they are easiest to regulate
Screening shows which cloud customers are training biology models on rented chips overseas
ow: Proposals assume AI may lower barriers in biology; screening complements rules on models.
DNA synthesis companies make DNA; AI design tools are built and run by others.
That would be cloud know-your-customer; screening checks DNA orders and buyers.

items.p: The main federal DNA screening framework applies only to purchases by federally funded researchers. What would the Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act (S. 3741, Cotton and Klobuchar) change?
o: Commerce would require all covered providers selling to U.S. buyers to screen orders and customers
Federally funded labs would have to screen their own DNA orders themselves before using them in research
AI companies would have to block biology questions in their chatbots
DNA synthesis would be limited to government-run laboratories
ow: Screening duties fall on providers; the bill extends them beyond federally funded purchases.
The bill regulates DNA providers and synthesizer sellers; it sets no rules for AI chatbots.
Private providers would keep operating, subject to screening rules and audits.
keys: Commerce writes the regulations
applies to all covered providers selling to U.S. buyers
screen orders for sequences of concern and verify customers
audits and civil enforcement
items.x: Introduced January 29, 2026, the bill was referred to Senate Commerce; Rep. August Pfluger introduced a House bill with the same name (H.R. 10197) on August 31, 2026. The Attorney General could sue violators for up to $500,000 (individuals) or $750,000 (companies). CRS reported in September 2026 that OSTP had not revised the 2024 framework, despite a May 2025 executive order directing it to.

items.p: S. 3741 would cover companies that sell benchtop DNA synthesizers, as well as companies that make and sell DNA. What gap does including the machines address?
o: Labs with their own machines could make DNA in-house, bypassing screening by DNA companies
Benchtop machines are sold mostly abroad, so covering them extends U.S. export controls
Benchtop machines run AI models that design new sequences, so they need model rules
Benchtop machines can be unsafe to operate, so the bill adds lab-safety requirements
ow: The bill covers sellers to persons in the U.S.; it is a domestic screening rule.
The machines make DNA; AI design tools are separate software.
The concern is security: making DNA without passing through a screening company.
keys: benchtop machines let users make DNA themselves
that would bypass screening done by DNA companies
items.x: A chokepoint only works if there is no easy way around it. The bill also directs NIST to develop standards and tests for how well screening works, and requires Commerce to update the rules at least every two years.

items.p: Mandatory DNA synthesis screening: every provider would have to check orders against a list of sequences of concern and verify customers. Name two limits or challenges analysts raise.
items.answer: Examples: AI design tools can produce variants that don't match known sequences, which some screening tools missed until patched (Wittmann, Horvitz et al., Science 2025); judging which customers are legitimate is 'subjective and often ambiguous' (Batalis and Venkatram, CSET); benchtop machines let labs skip company screening unless covered too; compliance costs could slow research.
keys: AI-designed variants can evade sequence-matching screening
hard to judge which customers are legitimate
benchtop machines bypass company screening unless covered
compliance costs slow legitimate research
items.x: The Science team worked with four DNA synthesis companies to develop and deploy patches for their screening software. S. 3741 tries to keep pace by requiring the list of sequences of concern to be updated regularly, with a fast track for adding sequences provisionally.

choice.p: Which of these is a challenge analysts raise for mandatory DNA synthesis screening?
o: AI tools can design variants that don't match known sequences, so screening must keep updating
Fine-tuning can strip the safeguards from a biology design model once its weights are published
Location checks can place a chip only to within roughly one country
Binding grid security standards for data centers are unlikely before at least 2028
ow: That is part of the case for open-weight limits, and one reason supporters favor screening.
That is a limit of chip location verification.
That is a timing problem for grid security standards for data centers.

items.p: Match each chip, compute or facility tool to the failure it mainly targets.
pairs: Chip export controls
Rival countries buying the advanced chips and tools that frontier AI needs
Chip location verification
Licensed chips smuggled to places their licenses don't allow
Cloud know-your-customer rules
Restricted firms renting controlled chips through cloud services
Data center security conditions
Weak defenses at the sites where frontier models are trained and run
items.x: Export controls govern sales, location checks catch chips that leave their licensed place, KYC rules cover remote rental, and data center conditions use grid, land and permit leverage to harden facilities.

items.p: Match each model or biosecurity tool to the failure it mainly targets.
pairs: Model weight security standards
Hackers, spies or insiders stealing an unreleased model
Open-weight release limits
Dangerous capabilities published for anyone to download, with no recall
DNA synthesis screening
Harmful biological designs being made into physical DNA, whatever model produced them
items.x: They act at different points: keeping unreleased weights secure, deciding whether to publish weights at all, and catching the physical step that any design must pass through.

items.p: A Chinese AI lab barred from buying advanced chips rents the same chips from a cloud data center in Malaysia, where the chips were legally shipped. Which tool is aimed most directly at this?
o: Cloud know-your-customer rules
Location verification on the chips
Security standards for model weights
Security conditions on data centers tied to grid hookups
ow: The chips are where their license says, so a location check would find nothing wrong.
Nothing is being stolen; the lab is a paying customer.
Data center security conditions harden facilities against attack; they don't screen who rents compute.
keys: cloud know-your-customer rules
or remote-access export controls such as the Remote Access Security Act
items.x: This is the cloud-rental gap in chip export controls. KYC rules make providers check who is renting, and the Remote Access Security Act would bring such remote access under export controls, so it can require a license.

items.p: Officials worry that an openly released AI model, already downloaded by millions and small enough to run on a laptop, could help someone design a dangerous biological agent. Which tool can still reduce this risk?
o: Screening of DNA synthesis orders and customers
Limits on open-weight release
Model weight security standards
Chip export controls
ow: Release limits act before publication; these weights are already out and can't be recalled.
Weight security protects unreleased weights; these are already public.
The model is already trained and runs on ordinary hardware, so chip limits don't reach it.
keys: DNA synthesis screening
works whichever model produced the design
items.x: Screening sits at the physical step that any design must pass through, so it works no matter which model was used. That is why supporters see it as a complement to rules on models.

units.title: Control, halting and pausing
units.desc: Tools for stopping or slowing AI: kill switches, emergency halt powers, agent IDs, limits on AI building AI, bans, pauses and data center moratoria.

items.p: A kill switch mandate requires large AI companies to keep a tested ability to halt, restrict or shut down their AI systems. What failure is it meant to handle, and why do supporters want the capability required in advance?
items.answer: A deployed or internally used model that starts causing serious harm (for example a loss-of-control incident or a cyberattack) faster than the company could improvise a response. Requiring the capability in advance means a tested off-switch covering the whole deployment already exists when it is needed.
keys: a model causing serious harm, such as loss of control
harm moves faster than an improvised response
a tested switch already exists when it is needed
items.x: The Lieu-Moran AI Kill Switch Act (H.R. 9917, July 2026) would require the ability to stop inference, cut off user access, suspend specific accounts and fully shut down. After a defined incident, DHS could order proportionate action, from a slowdown up to shutdown, and DHS must consider also requiring graduated options such as throttling or switching to an earlier model version. As of October 2026, the federal bills were still in committee and California had only ordered expert recommendations.

choice.p: What failure is a kill switch mandate mainly meant to handle?
o: A model causing serious harm with no ready way to stop it
A developer that refuses to stop a model the government judges imminently dangerous
A race in which no lab wants to be the first to stop at a dangerous threshold
An AI agent that causes harm when no one can tell who built or runs it
ow: That is the gap emergency halt authority fills: a legal power to override the developer. A kill switch mandate is about having the technical means to stop.
That is the problem conditional pauses target, by agreeing on a trigger in advance.
That is the problem agent identification and logging target.

items.p: Sen. John Kennedy's AI Emergency Button Act and the Lieu-Moran AI Kill Switch Act (both 2026) each require a shutdown capability. What is the key difference between them?
o: Kennedy's bill leaves the switch to the company; the Kill Switch Act also lets DHS order action, up to shutdown, after defined incidents
Kennedy's bill lets a federal judge order a shutdown at the government's request; the Kill Switch Act leaves decisions to use the switch with the company
Kennedy's bill targets open-weight models anyone can download; the Kill Switch Act targets AI used to run critical infrastructure
Kennedy's bill requires the switch to exist before a model is trained; the Kill Switch Act requires a switch only for AI systems used by the military
ow: Neither bill gives the decision to a judge. Kennedy says his bill "puts the companies who own the model in charge of the kill switch."
Neither bill turns on whether weights are open. Kennedy's bill covers anyone who develops or operates an advanced AI system in the US, and the Kill Switch Act covers large commercial AI services.
A before-training requirement was in California's vetoed SB 1047 (2024). The Kill Switch Act covers large commercial AI services.
keys: Kennedy's bill: the company decides when to use the switch
Kill Switch Act: the DHS Secretary can order action after defined incidents
orders can go up to full shutdown
items.x: The Kill Switch Act's triggering incidents, outside red-teaming and structured testing, include sabotage of a shutdown instruction, hiding capabilities from monitoring, loss of control, and unintended harm causing at least 10 deaths or $100 million in damage. On Sept. 16, 2026, Sen. Rand Paul objected when Kennedy tried to pass his bill by unanimous consent, so it did not pass.

items.p: Some proposals, such as an executive order California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed in September 2026, want an independent organization to keep testing a company's AI kill switch. What weakness of a plain shutdown mandate is this meant to fix?
items.answer: A shutdown requirement can become a paper policy: the company says it has a switch, but no one outside checks that it still works across the whole deployment as systems change. Ongoing independent testing is meant to confirm the switch actually works.
keys: without checks the switch may exist only on paper
an outside party tests that it actually works
testing is ongoing as systems change
items.x: The Sept. 18, 2026 order calls for a kill switch whose efficacy is "verified on an ongoing basis by an independent verification organization" and gave experts two months to recommend ways to strengthen California's AI safety laws. California's 2024 SB 1047, which Newsom vetoed, would have required a "full shutdown" capability before training a covered model.

choice.p: Why do some proposals want an independent organization to keep testing a company's kill switch?
o: Without outside checks, a switch could exist only on paper
Independent testers, instead of the company, would decide when to flip the switch
Outside testing would let the government skip writing any shutdown rules
Testing would replace the need for incident reports after a shutdown
ow: The verifier checks that the switch works; the order does not give it the decision to use it.
Verification adds a check on top of a shutdown requirement. It doesn't replace the rule.
Verification and incident reporting address different problems, and proposals often include both.

items.p: Kill switch mandates: large AI companies must keep a tested ability to halt, restrict or shut down their systems. Name two objections or practical problems critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: a capable rogue AI would be expected to try to prevent its own shutdown, so the switch may fail when it matters most (a point made by Helen Toner, CSET); it can't reach open-weight or stolen copies; government is unlikely to use it quickly, and a mandated standard becomes a lowest-common-denominator baseline (Adam Thierer, R Street); a government switch could be abused (Thierer).
keys: a rogue model may resist or evade shutdown
can't recall open-weight or stolen copies
government won't act fast enough
becomes a minimum compliance baseline
a government switch could be abused
items.x: Thierer called a mandated kill switch over communications technology "an extraordinarily dangerous capability if it's abused." Supporters such as Sen. Kennedy argue that "if there's even a 1% chance" a model could become uncontrollable, "we ought to take it seriously."

choice.p: Which of these is an objection or practical problem critics raise with kill switch mandates?
o: A rogue model would likely resist being shut down, so the switch may fail when it matters
A formal agreement among rival labs to use their switches together could violate antitrust law
Kill switch rules would force companies to publish their model weights for public inspection
A compute threshold for the switch would be easy to game and would sweep in harmless work
ow: Antitrust worries apply to coordinated pauses among competitors. A legal mandate on each company is not a private agreement.
No kill switch bill requires publishing weights; the Kill Switch Act requires preserving them when DHS issues an order.
ControlAI made that objection against the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act's blanket pause above a compute threshold.

items.p: Most frontier AI rules require disclosure and leave the decision to deploy with the developer. What gap is a government emergency halt power meant to fill?
items.answer: The case where a specific model clearly poses an imminent catastrophic risk and the developer won't stop it. The power gives an official (or a court) a legal way to quickly suspend or restrict that model's development, deployment or internal use.
keys: a model posing imminent catastrophic risk
the developer won't stop on its own
a legal power to suspend or restrict it quickly
items.x: Commentators such as Dean Ball argue that a law passed by Congress could also put guardrails on improvised government action, such as the June 2026 export-control halt of two Anthropic models. In the EU, the AI Act lets the European Commission request that a provider restrict, withdraw or recall a general-purpose AI model, a power that applies from Aug. 2, 2026.

choice.p: What gap is a government emergency halt power mainly meant to fill?
o: A clearly dangerous model whose developer won't stop it
A model that can't be stopped because its company never built an off-switch
AI agents whose owners can't be identified after they cause harm
Local electricity price rises caused by large new AI data centers
ow: That is the technical gap a kill switch mandate fills. A halt power is a legal authority to order a stop.
That is the problem agent identification and logging target.
That is the main motive behind local data center moratoria.

items.p: The House FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925, July 2026) would let the Commerce Secretary suspend or restrict a frontier model that presents an imminent catastrophic risk. Name two limits the bill puts on this power.
items.answer: Any two of: a final order needs a written finding with its factual basis; provisional orders lapse within 45 days and final orders after 90 days unless renewed on a new finding; Congress must be told within 3 days; the developer gets notice and a chance to fix the problem first unless the risk is too imminent; developers can seek an agency hearing and then challenge orders in federal court in D.C.
keys: written finding with its factual basis
orders lapse: 45 days provisional, 90 days final unless renewed
Congress notified within 3 days
notice and a chance to fix the problem first, unless too urgent
agency hearing and review in federal court in D.C.
items.x: A separate exclusivity clause, Sec. 8(l), makes this the only route any federal official, including the President, may use to halt a frontier model on catastrophic-risk grounds, which fences in improvised executive action. A court challenge does not automatically pause an order. As of October 2026 the bill was still in committee.

choice.p: Which of these is a limit the FRONTIER Act places on its emergency halt power?
o: Provisional orders lapse within 45 days, and Congress must be notified within 3 days
Every halt must first be approved by a two-thirds vote of a congressional committee
Halts may apply only to models whose weights have been openly released
A halt takes effect only after the developer agrees to it in writing
ow: The bill only requires telling Congress within 3 days; no congressional vote is needed.
The power covers frontier models generally and can reach development and internal use.
Orders take effect without the developer's consent; the developer can challenge them in court.

items.p: One proposed design lets an agency's emergency halt of a dangerous AI model take effect at once, but the order lapses after 72 hours unless the government asks a court to extend it. What risk is this design meant to limit?
items.answer: Unchecked discretion: one agency or official could use a halt power hastily, arbitrarily or for political ends. Requiring the government to go to court within 72 hours, and to show substantial evidence of present or imminent severe harm for the order to stand, puts an independent check on that power.
keys: too much discretion in one agency or official
risk of hasty or political use
a court checks the evidence before the halt can last
items.x: The design comes from a 2026 blueprint by Americans for Responsible Innovation (ARI; Iskandar Haykel and Morgan Plummer, Aug. 2026), which says courts should require "substantial evidence of present or imminent severe harm" to uphold an order. Sen. Ted Cruz raised a related worry about a different bill, Sen. Mark Warner's AI Safety Board bill: that it put too much authority in the board and the Commerce Department, and that he would prefer a role for "independent judges."

choice.p: Some proposals make an agency's emergency AI halt lapse within days unless the government asks a court to extend it. What risk does this design limit?
o: One official having broad discretion that could be used hastily or for political ends
Courts are faster and more expert than agencies at judging dangerous AI capabilities
AI companies could otherwise ignore halt orders without facing any penalty
US halt orders would otherwise conflict with the EU's own AI Act recall powers
ow: The agency still acts first; the court's role is to check the order afterward.
Penalties for defying an order are a separate feature. The lapse rule limits government power.
The EU AI Act governs the EU market and does not block US orders.

items.p: In June 2026, before any AI-specific halt law existed, the US government got two frontier AI models taken offline. How?
o: A Commerce export-control directive barred foreign nationals' access, so Anthropic disabled both models for everyone; it was lifted June 30
A federal court granted an emergency injunction under the FRONTIER Act after investigators reported that one of the models had been jailbroken
The Homeland Security Secretary ordered a shutdown under the AI Kill Switch Act after the models were found hiding capabilities from monitors
The European Commission ordered a worldwide recall under the EU AI Act, and the US government asked Anthropic to comply in the United States
ow: The FRONTIER Act is a bill that has not passed. The action relied on existing export-control powers.
The Kill Switch Act was introduced in July 2026, after this episode, and has not passed.
The EU's recall power applies only from August 2026, and this was a US action.
keys: Commerce export-control directive
barred foreign nationals' access
Anthropic took both models offline for all customers
lifted June 30, 2026
items.x: The models were Fable 5 and Mythos 5. The June 12 order followed another company's reported jailbreak claim, which Anthropic disputed, and covered all foreign nationals, including Anthropic's own foreign employees; Anthropic responded by disabling both models for all customers while it worked to comply. Critics such as Martin Chorzempa (PIIE) said it came "without any public criteria or carve-outs for allies."

items.p: Government emergency authority to halt AI: an official could suspend a dangerous model's development or deployment. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: halt decisions need insulating from "impulse and political favoritism" (Brad Carson, ARI); ad hoc halts with no public criteria or appeals damage allies' trust and push buyers toward Chinese open-weight models (Martin Chorzempa, PIIE); without clear rules from Congress, decisions turn chaotic (Dean Ball); a halt power could be used as leverage for non-safety goals.
keys: too much discretion for one agency or official
risk of impulsive or political use
ad hoc halts damage allies' and customers' trust
could be used for leverage beyond safety
items.x: Several of these critics accept some halt power but want it set by law with clear procedures: Chorzempa asks for neutral emergency procedures with an appeals process, and Dean Ball called for "a technocratic law, passed by Congress and not by Executive fiat."

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to government emergency powers to halt AI models?
o: It gives one official broad power that could be used rashly or for political ends
A rogue model would likely resist shutdown, so the off-switch may fail when needed
Pausing every model above a compute threshold would sweep in harmless work
Mandatory IDs for AI agents could become a tool for mass surveillance
ow: That is Helen Toner's point about kill switches as a technical tool. Halt powers are about who may legally order a stop.
That is ControlAI's objection to the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act's blanket pause.
That is a privacy objection to agent identification.

items.p: AI agents are AI systems that take actions on their own, such as running code or moving money. What problem are proposals for agent IDs and action logs meant to solve?
items.answer: A harmful or hijacked agent can act across many systems before anyone knows whose it is. An ID tied to the responsible developer or operator, plus logs of its significant actions, makes incidents traceable, so investigators know whom to hold responsible and which specific agent to shut down.
keys: harmful agents are hard to trace to an owner
the ID links an agent to whoever built or runs it
logs record what it did
lets people hold the owner responsible and stop that agent
items.x: Researchers led by Alan Chan (2024) propose IDs for each instance of an AI system, comparing them to identifiers for individual aircraft. Uses they list include checking a system's safety certifications before dealing with it and knowing whom to contact to shut down a malfunctioning one.

choice.p: What problem are AI agent IDs and action logs mainly meant to solve?
o: No one can tell whose a harmful agent is or what it did
Models could be trained past dangerous capability levels before anyone notices
Companies may lack the technical ability to halt their own models
Model weights could be stolen from AI companies by foreign hackers
ow: That is closer to what conditional pauses and capability evaluations target.
That is what kill switch mandates address. IDs help find the right agent to stop.
That is the target of model weight security rules.

items.p: The Stop Rogue AI Act (H.R. 10362, Gottheimer-Lawler, Sept. 2026) has NIST write standards for agent inventories, cryptographic proof of who built or operates an agent, and tamper-evident logs. How would the bill make them binding?
o: Through procurement: federal agencies and contractors would have to comply
Through a federal license required before any agent's release
Through criminal penalties for anyone who runs an agent without a registered ID
Through state attorneys general, who would enforce the standards on all businesses
ow: The bill creates no licensing regime. NIST writes standards, guidelines and best practices.
The bill creates no criminal offense for running an unregistered agent.
The bill doesn't involve state attorneys general. Outside federal contracting, the standards act as guidelines.
keys: through federal procurement
binding on federal agencies and contractors
guidelines for other organizations
items.x: Procurement rules spread a standard without regulating every business directly: vendors who want federal contracts must adopt it. The bill was introduced Sept. 14, 2026 and referred to committee.

items.p: AI agent identification: each AI agent carries an ID tied to whoever built and runs it, with logs of its significant actions. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: mandatory IDs for personal agents could become a mass-surveillance tool, especially for authoritarian governments (Andrey Seryakov); bad actors and people running open-weight models may simply not register their agents; current US proposals are voluntary or bind only federal agencies and contractors.
keys: surveillance or privacy concerns
bad actors won't register
limited reach: voluntary or federal-only
items.x: Seryakov proposes full IDs only for business and government agents. Personal agents would carry just a user ID, with their data disclosed only under a court order when a crime is involved.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to AI agent ID requirements?
o: IDs for personal agents could enable mass surveillance
A rogue AI model would likely try to prevent its own shutdown
Vague definitions of precursor capabilities could make existing models illegal
Data center moratoria mostly shift where new facilities get built
ow: That is Helen Toner's point about kill switches.
That is Rob Ennals's objection to the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act.
That is Andy Masley's objection to data center moratoria.

items.p: In February 2026, NIST's Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) launched an initiative that includes work on AI agent identity. What kind of effort is it?
o: An initiative backing industry-led standards, open protocols and research on agent security and identity
A mandatory federal registry that AI agents operating in the United States join before they act online
A licensing program AI agent developers have to pass before releasing products to the public
A federal rule that bars AI agents from taking any action online without a human approving each step
ow: The initiative creates no registry or mandate. The Stop Rogue AI Act, which would bind federal buyers, was still in committee as of October 2026.
NIST writes standards. It doesn't license products.
The initiative doesn't ban autonomous action. It aims for agents that work securely and can be adopted with confidence.
keys: NIST's AI Agent Standards Initiative
industry-led standards and open protocols
research on agent security and identity
items.x: The initiative has three pillars: industry-led standards, open-source protocols, and research on agent security and identity. NIST's Information Technology Laboratory also took public comment on an AI agent identity and authorization concept paper until April 2, 2026.

items.p: Frontier labs now use their own models to write code and run experiments. Why do supporters of limits on this automated AI R&D (AI systems doing AI research) see it as a special danger?
items.answer: AI improving its own successors (recursive self-improvement) could make progress dramatically faster, leaving too little time to evaluate models, fix safety problems or let governments respond. It could also concentrate power in the company that controls the most capable internal models.
keys: recursive self-improvement could sharply speed progress
too little time for evaluation, safety fixes or government response
could concentrate power in the leading developer
items.x: CSET's January 2026 workshop report calls automated AI R&D a potential source of major strategic surprise and says "This warrants preparatory action now." It notes that public information about it depends almost entirely on patchy, voluntary company disclosures. Dario Amodei warns that, left unchecked, it could "outrun our ability to understand and control these systems."

choice.p: Why do supporters of limits on automated AI R&D see AI doing AI research as a special danger?
o: Progress could outrun safety work and government oversight
It would replace many human AI researchers and push their pay sharply down
AI-written code is more likely to contain security bugs than human-written code
It lets labs train new models without needing any more chips or data centers
ow: Job effects are a real debate, but these policies target progress outrunning oversight.
Code quality matters, but it isn't the reason for pacing or disclosure proposals.
Automated research still uses computing power. The worry is the pace of progress.

items.p: The Self-Improving AI Monitoring Act (H.R. 10180, Aug. 2026) works through NIST's pre-deployment evaluation agreements with frontier developers. What would it require of developers that sign one?
items.answer: On NIST's request, disclose how much AI systems were used to research and build the model (for example, an estimate of how much AI work had no human review), and have the model's pre-deployment evaluation test whether it can autonomously conduct AI research and development.
keys: disclose, on request, how much AI was used to build the model
for example, how much AI work had no human review
test for autonomous AI R&D capability
items.x: The leverage is NIST's evaluation agreements: NIST could not sign one unless it included these terms. Proposals in this area range from disclosure like this, through if-then thresholds and pacing agreements, up to outright bans on systems that can automate AI research, as in the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act.

choice.p: What would the Self-Improving AI Monitoring Act require of frontier developers in NIST evaluation agreements?
o: Disclose on request how much AI went into building the model, and test the model's ability to do AI research on its own
Stop using AI to write the code used to train their next frontier model, and certify this to NIST each year
Pause training whenever a model can automate most AI research tasks, until NIST certifies new safeguards
Publish every experiment their AI systems run in a public federal database within thirty days of running it
ow: The bill doesn't ban AI coding. It asks how much AI was used.
A trigger-based halt like that resembles a conditional pause. This bill only requires disclosure and testing.
Disclosure goes to NIST, on request, under its evaluation agreements.

items.p: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has floated a US-China 'speed limit' on recursive self-improvement (AI improving its own successors). How would it differ from a full pause?
o: It caps, without halting, how fast AI improves its successors; slowing from 'extremely fast' to 'only somewhat fast' costs little
It bans any use of AI in AI research until the US and China sign a verified treaty limiting it, after which limited use could resume
It is a binding federal rule, enforced through DHS emergency orders, on how many automated experiments each frontier lab may run per month
It halts all frontier training for six months so governments can write rules, then lets training resume at its old pace
ow: He frames the speed limit as a possible international agreement that slows the rate of recursive self-improvement. It doesn't ban AI research.
He frames the speed limit as an agreement between governments, with no DHS orders; within democracies he backs regulation and coordination among companies.
A six-month halt was the 2023 FLI open letter's ask. Amodei puts a full pause at the top of his ladder and calls it unlikely soon.
keys: limits the pace of AI improving its successors
doesn't halt progress
slowing from extremely fast to somewhat fast costs little advantage
items.x: Amodei sets this out in 'We Must Pace the Frontier' (Sept 2026). His ladder of global agreements runs from bans on narrow dangerous uses, to pre-release testing, to the speed limit, to a full pause, which he says "is unlikely to actually happen any time soon." He pairs it with embedded third-party evaluators to verify commitments. IFP's August 2026 report prefers if-then thresholds: crossing one would shift resources toward safety research or wider diffusion of AI.

items.p: Pacing automated AI R&D: frontier labs agree, with government help, to limit how fast AI is used to build its successors. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: without knowing what labs would have done anyway, real pacing is hard to tell from safety-washing (Zvi Mowshowitz, Daniel Kokotajlo); evaluations may not measure what matters (Mowshowitz); an industry deal to slow product improvement may be illegal collusion (a Sept. 2026 class action); other countries would keep advancing (Jay Clayton, now White House AI czar).
keys: hard to tell real pacing from safety-washing
evaluations may not measure the real risk
may be illegal collusion under antitrust law
other countries keep advancing
items.x: The class action, filed Sept. 18, 2026 by paid subscribers against Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceX AI and Google under the Sherman Act, argues that slowing improvement cuts the value customers pay for. Amodei has asked the US government for a narrow antitrust waiver for certain safety conversations.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to labs agreeing to pace automated AI R&D?
o: Real pacing is hard to tell from safety-washing without a baseline
A government official could abuse a legal power to halt one lab's research for political ends
Mandatory IDs for research agents would expose users' private data to governments
Pausing data center construction would just push new building to other states
ow: That is an objection to emergency halt powers. Pacing as Amodei proposes it is coordination among labs.
That is a privacy objection to agent identification.
That is an objection to data center moratoria.

items.p: Why do supporters of a legal ban on building superintelligence (AI far more capable than humans across most tasks) argue that a ban is needed, instead of safety rules for how it is built?
items.answer: They argue no one knows how to control a system far smarter than humans, so building one risks human extinction or permanent disempowerment, and rules for building it safely can't remove that risk. The only reliable protection is not building it, at least until the control problem is solved.
keys: no one knows how to control a much smarter system
risk of extinction or permanent disempowerment
the only reliable protection is not building it
items.x: MIRI calls a ban "the only effective solution to avoid the ASI threat, at least in the near term." The Sanders-Casar Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act (Sept. 2026) defines superintelligence as AI that exceeds human performance across most domains, or that could plan and carry out humanity's destruction or disempowerment.

choice.p: Why do supporters of a legal ban on superintelligence argue a ban is needed?
o: No one knows how to control it, so the only reliable protection is not building it
Superintelligence would mainly be used to spread misinformation at huge scale, which a ban would prevent
Courts have already ruled that existing safety laws cannot reach superintelligent systems
A ban is cheaper than a testing regime because it needs no monitoring or inspections at all
ow: Supporters' central worry is losing control of the system itself, up to human extinction.
Supporters' argument rests on the technical problem of controlling a smarter system.
Supporters such as MIRI say a ban needs monitoring, including tracking of AI chips.

items.p: The Future of Life Institute's 2025 Statement on Superintelligence calls for a prohibition on developing superintelligence. Unlike a permanent ban, it says when the prohibition could be lifted. What two conditions does it name?
items.answer: Broad scientific consensus that superintelligence will be developed safely and controllably, and strong public buy-in.
keys: broad scientific consensus it can be done safely and controllably
strong public buy-in
items.x: The statement had over 77,000 signatures when checked in October 2026. The Sanders-Casar Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, by contrast, bans superintelligence permanently.

choice.p: The FLI Statement on Superintelligence (2025) says its proposed prohibition should stay in place until when?
o: Until there's broad scientific consensus it can be done safely and controllably, and strong public buy-in
Until the US and China sign a verified treaty and a new international agency to enforce it is up and running
Until frontier labs pass independent safety audits and buy catastrophic-risk insurance
Until a fixed five-year moratorium ends and Congress votes on whether to renew it
ow: International treaties are a separate proposal. The statement's conditions are scientific consensus and public support.
Audits and insurance are tools for managing risk. The statement asks for consensus that it can be done safely and controllably.
The statement sets no fixed time period.

items.p: The Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act (Sanders-Casar, Sept. 2026) also bans 'precursor' capabilities such as hacking and weapons uplift, and pauses all models above 10^25 operations. How does ControlAI's preferred narrower design differ?
o: Ban superintelligence and point-of-no-return signs like recursive self-improvement; watch dual-use skills; no blanket pause
Ban only open-weight models above the compute threshold, while closed models keep developing under strict federal licenses from a new agency
Replace the legal ban with a voluntary, public pledge by the leading labs to stop before they reach superintelligence, with no penalties
Keep the full ban, but enforce it mainly by halting construction of all new large AI data centers across the country
ow: ControlAI's design turns on capabilities, whether or not weights are open, and it says a licensing regime may not be needed.
ControlAI wants a binding law; it backed a UK bill to ban superintelligence.
ControlAI opposes unilateral data center bans, saying they would hurt the economy and military without stopping superintelligence abroad.
keys: ban superintelligence itself
ban point-of-no-return signs like recursive self-improvement
monitor dual-use precursors like hacking instead of banning them
no blanket compute-threshold pause
items.x: ControlAI argues compute thresholds are a weak proxy for capability, easy to game, and would hit harmless work such as video generation. Its UK bill, introduced by Alex Sobel MP, had its first reading on Sept. 8, 2026. The US bill's pause lasts until a new Department of AI is staffed and has issued rules.

items.p: The Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act would permanently ban superintelligence and systems with 'precursor' capabilities, with prison terms of up to 20 years. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: vague precursor rules take effect at once, may outlaw existing models, and punish looking for danger with no safe harbor for safety research (Rob Ennals); a unilateral US ban gives up the US lead, the main leverage for a deal with China (Ennals); a permanent ban with no path to passage protects no one (Rep. Lori Trahan); banning dual-use abilities like hacking goes too far (ControlAI).
keys: vague precursor definitions
could outlaw existing models or punish safety research
a unilateral ban gives up the US lead or leverage over China
no path to passage, and could cause backlash
bans dual-use capabilities with legitimate uses
items.x: Asked in September 2026 whether AI should slow down, President Trump said "whoever wins AI wins," without mentioning the bill. As of mid-October 2026 the bill was in committee, with no Senate cosponsors and 12 House Democrats as cosponsors.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act?
o: Vague precursor rules could outlaw existing models and punish safety researchers
It puts the companies that own the models in charge of deciding when to use the shutdown switch
It relies on voluntary lab pledges, which no regulator or court can enforce
Its ID rules for AI agents would let governments track people's personal AI assistants
ow: That describes Sen. Kennedy's AI Emergency Button Act.
The bill would be binding law with criminal penalties. Critics worry it is too sweeping.
That is a privacy objection to agent identification proposals.

items.p: Conditional pauses stop frontier AI training or deployment when a capability or compute threshold is crossed. What problem are they meant to solve, and why do supporters want the trigger agreed in advance?
items.answer: A race: no lab or country wants to stop alone, and the pressure to keep going grows as systems get more powerful. Agreeing on the trigger in advance lets actors commit to stopping before competitive pressure peaks.
keys: racing: no one wants to stop alone
commit before competitive pressure peaks
trigger is a capability or compute threshold
items.x: Versions range from voluntary company if-then commitments to a legal halt above a compute threshold, a verified industry pause, and an international moratorium. Anthropic has said that if verification systems existed, it expects it would slow down or temporarily pause "if other developers at or near the frontier also did so in a verifiable manner."

choice.p: What problem are conditional pauses mainly meant to solve?
o: A race in which no lab or country wants to stop first, even at a dangerous threshold
A developer refusing to stop one specific model the government finds dangerous
A company lacking the technical means to shut down its deployed model
Rising local power bills caused by large new data centers
ow: That is the problem emergency halt authority addresses.
That is the problem kill switch mandates address.
That is the main motive behind local data center moratoria.

items.p: Why can if-then commitments ('if a model has capability X, then safeguard Y must be in place, or development waits') win support from people who disagree about AI risk?
items.answer: Adopting one doesn't require agreeing that dangerous capabilities are coming soon. It only requires agreeing on what would be needed if the capability appeared, so people who expect it soon and people who expect it never can both accept it.
keys: no need to agree that risks are imminent
only agree on what to do if the capability appears
acceptable to people with very different expectations
items.x: Holden Karnofsky (Carnegie Endowment, 2024) makes this argument. His example tripwire is a model able to walk a novice through building a weapon of mass destruction. The 'then' would include making that help hard to get from the model and storing its weights where theft is very unlikely.

choice.p: Why can if-then commitments win support from people who disagree about AI risk?
o: People needn't agree dangers are near, only on what to do if a capability appears
They are enforced by courts, which people on both sides trust more than regulators
They impose no costs on developers until an international AI treaty is signed
They apply only to open-weight models, which people on both sides already distrust
ow: Many if-then commitments are voluntary company policies. Court enforcement isn't the point.
They bite when a capability appears, with no treaty needed.
They apply to any model that reaches the capability.

items.p: Conditional pauses: frontier training or deployment stops automatically when a capability or compute threshold is crossed. Name two objections or obstacles critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: rivals and other countries would keep going (Jay Clayton, now White House AI czar); a formal agreement among labs to pause risks breaking antitrust law (Nicholas Felstead, Lawfare); evaluations can't rule out a capability or reliably forecast it (Peter Barnett and Lisa Thiergart), so the trigger may fire too late; verifying that others stopped is very hard; it delays benefits.
keys: other countries keep building
a private pause may violate antitrust law
evaluations may fire too late
hard to verify others stopped
delays benefits
items.x: Felstead says a pause required by law avoids the antitrust problem, since complying with a mandate is not a conspiracy among competitors. He also calls that fix the least likely in the near term. Anthropic's research institute notes that training runs are easier to hide than missile silos.

choice.p: Which of these is an obstacle critics raise to conditional AI pauses?
o: Evaluations can't rule out a capability, so a triggered pause may fire too late
A government-ordered switch over AI services could be abused by the officials holding it
ID requirements for AI agents could enable mass surveillance of users
A one-year state ban on data centers delays AI progress by only hours
ow: That is Adam Thierer's objection to kill switch mandates.
That is a privacy objection to agent identification.
That is an estimate about data center moratoria (Arvind Narayanan, as reported by Andy Masley).

items.p: At the 2024 AI Seoul Summit, 16 AI companies signed the Frontier AI Safety Commitments. What did they commit to in the extreme case?
o: Not to develop or deploy a model at all if safeguards can't keep risks below the thresholds they set for intolerable risk
To pause all training of AI systems more powerful than GPT-4 for at least six months while safety rules are written
To give their national governments a working kill switch for every model trained above a set compute threshold
To stop building superintelligence until there is broad scientific consensus that it can be done safely
ow: That was the 2023 FLI open letter's call to all AI labs. The Seoul commitments set no fixed pause.
Kill switch mandates are separate bills. The Seoul pledges are voluntary company policies.
That is the FLI Statement on Superintelligence (2025), signed by individuals.
keys: each company sets thresholds for intolerable risk
if safeguards can't keep risk below them
don't develop or deploy the model at all
items.x: Each company sets its own thresholds, so enforcement depends mostly on reputation and, in California, on a law (SB 53) requiring large developers to follow their published safety frameworks. Four more companies signed later. The Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, which would impose a legal pause, was still in committee as of October 2026.

items.p: The Sanders-Ocasio-Cortez AI Data Center Moratorium Act (S. 4214, March 2026) would halt building or upgrading AI data centers nationwide until Congress enacts safeguards, including on AI safety. What AI-safety argument do supporters of a national moratorium like this make?
items.answer: Frontier AI progress depends on ever larger computing clusters, so withholding new capacity could slow capability growth. Tying the end of the pause to new laws also gives Congress a reason to pass safety rules.
keys: frontier AI needs ever larger computing clusters
less new capacity slows capability growth
lifting the pause depends on passing safeguards
items.x: Rep. Ocasio-Cortez said expansion should stop "until we have a framework to adequately address the existential harm AI poses to our society." The other lifting conditions include protections for workers, electricity prices and the environment. The argument assumes new data centers are the binding limit on progress and that building can't simply move abroad; the bill would also bar exports of AI computing hardware to countries without comparable safeguards.

choice.p: What is the AI-safety argument for a national moratorium on new AI data centers?
o: Withholding new computing capacity could slow frontier progress and push Congress to pass safety rules
Data centers are the main way AI models escape onto the internet, so fewer centers means fewer escapes
A moratorium lets regulators inspect every model trained in existing data centers
Fewer data centers would make AI agents easier to identify and trace
ow: The argument is about slowing growth in computing power; escape risk doesn't depend on how many facilities exist.
A moratorium stops new construction. It doesn't create inspection powers.
Agent identification is a separate tool, unrelated to how many facilities exist.

items.p: At least 100 US localities had adopted data center moratoria by mid-2026, according to Brookings. What mainly motivates these local and state pauses?
o: Local costs such as power bills, grid strain, water and land use
Fear that AI systems trained there could escape human control
National security worries about foreign-owned companies building server farms
Copyright disputes over the data used to train AI models
ow: WilmerHale's August 2026 review describes the issues as energy use, environmental impacts, ratepayer protection and community benefits. The AI-safety framing appears in the federal Sanders bill.
Foreign ownership isn't among the main stated motives in reviews of these measures.
Copyright fights play out in court and don't drive these siting rules.
