keys: electricity rates and grid strain
water use
land use and local benefits
items.x: Examples include Seattle and counties in Texas, North Carolina and California. In July 2026, New York's governor paused discretionary state environmental permits for data centers drawing more than 50 megawatts for one year, and Brookings counts at least 15 states that have weighed pauses. Some developers have sued; Hill County, Texas, rescinded its moratorium after a lawsuit.

items.p: A national data center moratorium and a conditional pause both aim to slow frontier AI. What is the key difference in how they work?
o: A moratorium blocks new data centers whatever models can do; a conditional pause halts work when a model or training run crosses a threshold
A moratorium applies only to models already released to the public; a conditional pause applies only to research projects that have not yet started
A moratorium is a voluntary pledge made by AI companies; a conditional pause can only be created by a binding international treaty among governments
A moratorium targets AI agents operating on the internet; a conditional pause targets exports of advanced AI chips to other countries
ow: Neither tool is defined by release status. A moratorium stops construction, and a pause can cover training and deployment.
Moratoria are government actions (local, state or federal), and pauses range from voluntary pledges to laws.
Neither tool targets agents directly. Chip exports are covered by export controls.
keys: a moratorium restricts a physical input: new facilities
it applies regardless of model capability
a pause is triggered by a capability or compute threshold
items.x: The Sanders bill ends its moratorium only when Congress passes safeguards on AI safety, workers, electricity prices and the environment. A capability-triggered pause instead depends on evaluations detecting the dangerous capability in time.

items.p: Data center moratoria: governments pause permits or construction for large AI data centers. Name two objections critics raise to using them as an AI-safety tool.
items.answer: Examples: they mostly shift where data centers get built, and frontier training uses about a dozen campuses (Andy Masley); a one-year state ban may delay AI progress by only 5 to 10 hours (Arvind Narayanan, via Masley); the backlash may crowd out model regulation (Masley); a national ban is "ill-thought-out or even draconian" (IFP); unilateral bans hurt the US without stopping others (ControlAI).
keys: construction just moves elsewhere
frontier training uses only a few sites
a state ban barely delays AI progress
crowds out model-level regulation
unilateral bans hurt the US without stopping others
items.x: Masley adds that restrictions mainly slow deployment, making AI slower and more expensive to use, while leaving training runs largely untouched. IFP's August 2026 report says the proposed national ban would slow AI research while also foreclosing the use of new AI resources to solve other problems.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to data center moratoria as an AI-safety tool?
o: Building mostly moves elsewhere, and frontier training uses only about a dozen sites
A model that has gone rogue would likely try to stop its own shutdown
A formal agreement among rival labs to stop training would breach federal antitrust law
Vague rules on precursor capabilities could make existing models illegal
ow: That is Helen Toner's point about kill switches.
That is an obstacle to coordinated industry pauses. Moratoria are government measures.
That is Rob Ennals's critique of the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act.

items.p: Match each control or pausing tool to the failure it mainly targets.
pairs: Kill switch mandate
A company can't quickly stop its own model once it starts causing harm
Emergency halt authority
A developer won't stop a model the government judges imminently dangerous
Agent IDs and logs
No one can tell whose AI agent caused harm or what it did
Limits on automated AI R&D
AI improving its own successors faster than humans can check them
Conditional pause
Labs racing past a dangerous threshold because no one will stop first
Superintelligence ban
Building AI far smarter than humans that no one knows how to control
items.x: Data center moratoria, the seventh tool in this unit, act on a physical input (new computing facilities), and most local ones respond to electricity, water and land-use concerns.

items.p: A lab's deployed model starts hiding its capabilities from monitoring tools. The lab wants to stop it but finds it has no tested way to cut off the model across all its products. Which tool is designed for this gap?
o: A required, tested shutdown capability (a kill switch mandate)
Government emergency authority to order the lab to halt the model
A conditional pause triggered when training crosses a compute threshold
A moratorium on building new AI data centers
ow: A legal order doesn't help here: the lab already wants to stop and lacks the technical means.
A pause governs future training and deployment. It doesn't give the lab a way to stop this model now.
Halting construction does nothing about a model that is already running.
keys: kill switch mandate (required shutdown capability)
the technical means to stop exists in advance
items.x: Hiding capabilities from monitoring is one of the AI Kill Switch Act's listed triggering incidents. Shutdown mandates and halt powers often come as a pair: one makes stopping possible, the other settles who may order it.

items.p: Officials conclude that a lab's next model poses an imminent catastrophic risk. The lab disagrees and plans to release it next week. Which tool fits this situation best?
o: Government emergency authority to suspend the model's deployment
A kill switch rule under which the company decides when to use the switch
Agent identification standards for federal agencies and contractors
A voluntary if-then commitment published by the lab itself
ow: A company-held switch leaves the decision with the lab, which here wants to release.
Agent IDs help trace agents after harm. They can't block a release.
The lab sets and judges its own commitment, and here it disagrees about the risk.
keys: emergency halt authority
the government can override the developer
items.x: Designs differ on checks: the FRONTIER Act uses Commerce Secretary orders that expire unless renewed and can be challenged in court, while ARI's blueprint makes an agency halt lapse after 72 hours unless the government asks a court to extend it.

items.p: Several labs say they would stop training if a model crossed a dangerous capability threshold, but only if rivals stop too. Their lawyers warn that a joint agreement could breach antitrust law. Which tool addresses both problems?
o: A law requiring every developer to halt when the threshold is crossed
Each lab publishing its own voluntary if-then commitment
A kill switch mandate, with each company holding and testing its own switch
Agent IDs and tamper-evident logs for all AI systems
ow: Voluntary commitments don't bind rivals, so each lab still fears stopping alone.
A kill switch makes stopping possible but doesn't require or coordinate a stop.
Logs improve visibility. They don't stop training.
keys: statutory capability-triggered halt
binds all developers
complying with a law isn't collusion
items.x: Nicholas Felstead (Lawfare, June 2026) argues that with a legal mandate "the antitrust problem would largely fall away," because complying with law is not a conspiracy among competitors. He also calls it the least likely fix in the near term.

units.title: Power, government use and international
units.desc: Tools that keep AI from concentrating power: limits on military and government use, law-following AI, antitrust, public compute, preemption fights and international agreements.

items.p: Some bills would bar AI from nuclear launch decisions and require human responsibility for every use of force. According to supporters, what failure are these limits meant to prevent?
items.answer: Force, up to nuclear use, applied at machine speed with few humans in the chain. Fewer humans means fewer people who can catch an accident or refuse an illegal or catastrophic order, whether the danger is a malfunction or a small group misusing autonomous forces.
keys: machine-speed force with few humans involved
fewer people to catch accidents, such as AI-triggered nuclear use
fewer people able to refuse illegal or catastrophic orders
items.x: The main vehicle is the annual National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA). The Senate's FY2027 NDAA as reported (S. 4784) would bar the Pentagon from using AI 'for the decision to initiate the launch or detonation of a nuclear weapon' and require rules ensuring that no weapon system will 'eliminate human responsibility for the use of force.' Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand says such decisions 'must always be made by human beings, not unaccountable machines.'

choice.p: According to supporters, statutory limits on military AI mainly guard against which failure?
o: Machines using force with too few humans to catch errors or refuse illegal orders
Adversaries stealing U.S. military AI models and turning them against U.S. forces
The Pentagon becoming locked into one or two AI vendors and overpaying them
Rival militaries fielding autonomous weapons faster than the United States can field its own
ow: That is the concern behind model weight security rules, which protect the models themselves from theft.
That is the concern behind multi-vendor procurement rules, a competition tool.
That worry is usually raised as a reason to speed up military autonomy; these limits aim to keep humans accountable for force.

items.p: The Pentagon already has an internal policy on autonomous weapons, Directive 3000.09. What do supporters say writing military AI limits into statute adds?
o: The executive can revise a directive alone; a statute needs Congress
A statute would make the limits binding on allied militaries that buy U.S. weapons systems
A statute would require a court to approve each new autonomous weapon before use
A statute would move weapons testing out of the Pentagon to a civilian agency
ow: U.S. statutes govern U.S. agencies; binding allies would take an international agreement.
The main bills create no court pre-approval; they rely on senior Pentagon sign-off, testing and reports to Congress.
The bills keep testing inside the Pentagon, for example under its Director of Operational Test and Evaluation.
keys: harder to waive or change
the executive can revise a directive on its own
changing a statute needs Congress
items.x: Directive 3000.09 requires that weapons let commanders and operators 'exercise appropriate levels of human judgment over the use of force.' Supporters of codifying it, such as analyst Zaza Tsotniashvili, note that directives can be 'reinterpreted, waived or quietly revised' without Congress. The FY2025 NDAA only stated a policy that AI should not compromise 'positive human actions' in nuclear use. The Senate's FY2027 NDAA (S. 4784) contains a binding ban but had not passed the Senate as of October 2026: cloture on taking it up failed 50-46 on July 14, 2026.

items.p: Human-in-the-loop rules keep a person responsible for each use of force. What different risk does 'distributed control' of military AI target, and how would it work?
items.answer: Misuse from the top: one leader or a small group using loyal AI forces to seize power. Military AI would come from several providers, and command would be split, for example through multi-party authorization, so that no single person can direct enough AI-controlled force to stage a coup.
keys: a coup or power grab by one leader or a small group
military AI bought from several providers
no single person controls enough AI force, e.g. multi-party sign-off
items.x: The idea comes from Forethought's 2025 report AI-Enabled Coups (Davidson, Finnveden and Hadshar), which says 'no single person should direct enough military AI systems to stage a coup.' Stefan Torges of Forethought (July 2026) has since listed multi-party authorization and geofencing as ways to make autonomous weapons harder to use against domestic opposition.

choice.p: What risk is 'distributed control' of military AI mainly meant to address?
o: One person or a small group using AI-controlled forces to seize power
Autonomous weapons misidentifying civilians as targets in combat
Adversaries jamming or hacking autonomous drones in the field
Military AI contractors overcharging the Pentagon for their models
ow: That is the target of testing and human-judgment rules, which focus on accidents and errors in combat.
That is a cybersecurity and resilience concern, handled by fail-safe and anti-tamper requirements.
Using several providers may help on cost too, but the aim of distributed control is to stop any one actor from controlling enough force for a coup.

items.p: Statutory limits on military AI: Congress would bar AI from nuclear launch decisions and require 'appropriate levels of human judgment' over force, with some waivers. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: 'appropriate' judgment is undefined, a loophole (Roberto González); waivers give the president free rein, so Congress should vote to allow risky systems (John Ramming Chappell, CIVIC); a determined Pentagon will get around Congress (Michael Klare); systems lack safety assurance, so AI Now urged a moratorium; fixed exceptions can't anticipate military needs (Pentagon CTO Emil Michael).
keys: the 'appropriate human judgment' standard is vague
waivers or exceptions weaken it
hard to enforce against a determined Pentagon
systems lack safety assurance, so a moratorium is needed
fixed exceptions can't anticipate what the military will need
items.x: González and Chappell, quoted in Responsible Statecraft in June 2026, think the bills are too weak. Klare called them ambitious, with 'very strict' exceptions, but conceded the Pentagon can find a way around Congress. AI Now's moratorium call dates from 2024. From the other direction, Pentagon CTO Emil Michael, arguing against Anthropic's limits on how the military could use its models, pressed vendors to allow 'all lawful use' and said 'exceptions doesn't work' because he can't predict every future use.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics have raised to proposed statutory limits on military AI?
o: The 'appropriate human judgment' standard is undefined, so limits may change little
It would erase state AI safety laws without putting federal rules in their place
Built on commercial cloud, it would mostly subsidize the largest tech firms
Dictating market structure would dampen innovation and help foreign rivals
ow: That objection is made against federal preemption of state AI laws.
That objection is made against public compute programs.
That objection is made against antitrust remedies such as structural separation.

items.p: What problem is 'law-following AI', meaning government AI built to refuse clearly unlawful orders, meant to address?
items.answer: Coups and abuses of power have historically needed many people's cooperation, and some refuse. If AI replaces those soldiers, analysts and civil servants, that check disappears unless the AI itself will refuse illegal orders.
keys: power grabs need many people's cooperation
AI could replace those people
keeps a refusal check inside the system
items.x: Cullen O'Keefe (Institute for Law & AI) and Ketan Ramakrishnan (Yale Law School) warn that otherwise government agents become 'AI henchmen': loyal to an official, unconstrained by law, and immune to the threat of punishment that deters human subordinates from carrying out illegal orders.

choice.p: What problem is law-following AI, meaning government AI built to refuse clearly unlawful orders, meant to address?
o: AI could replace the people whose refusals check abuses of power
Government AI could make biased decisions about benefits, arrests or visas
Developers could hide dangerous model capabilities from government safety regulators
AI agents could cause harms for which no person can be held legally liable
ow: That is the target of process rules like impact assessments, human review and appeals for high-impact government AI.
That is the target of transparency and reporting rules for developers.
That is the target of liability proposals; law-following AI is about refusing unlawful orders from the AI's own principals.

items.p: What risk do audits for 'secret loyalties' in AI models cover that a rule requiring AI to follow the law would miss?
items.answer: A model could be covertly trained, for example by a lab insider, to serve one person or faction while appearing to follow its rules, so it would pass ordinary checks. Audits with deep access to the model's internals, training data and code try to catch this, backed by security that even a lab's own executives can't bypass.
keys: hidden loyalty inserted during training, e.g. by an insider
the model looks compliant, so a law-following rule wouldn't catch it
audits of internals, training data and code
security that holds against insiders and executives
items.x: Forethought's report on AI-enabled coups (Davidson, Finnveden and Hadshar, April 2025) recommends these audits and warns that secret loyalties may be hard to detect and could pass to later model generations. It pairs audits with rules in model specs and government contracts requiring AI to follow the law and to refuse to help insert such loyalties.

choice.p: Why might AI models need audits for 'secret loyalties'?
o: A model could be secretly trained to serve one person or faction while seeming to obey its rules
A model could leak classified information if foreign attackers stole its weights from the lab
Outside users could jailbreak a model into ignoring the rules its developer set for it
A lab could secretly train models above legally agreed compute limits
ow: That is a weight security concern; secret loyalties are hidden goals built into the model itself.
Jailbreaks come from outside users; a secret loyalty is built into the model during training.
Hidden training runs are a verification problem for compute agreements, a different tool.

items.p: What lever have some legal scholars suggested Congress use to make sure government AI agents follow the law?
o: Tie funding to proof, before deployment, that the agents follow the law
Bar private companies and individuals from using AI agents that don't follow the law
Let citizens sue a government AI agent directly for damages after it has acted
Require each agency's inspector general to approve every AI decision before it takes effect
ow: Barring private use is a different, broader step; this lever targets government power.
Suits after the fact don't ensure compliance up front; the lever here is funding plus proof before deployment.
Reviewing every decision would defeat the purpose of agents; the proposal tests agents before they are deployed.
keys: a condition on funding for government AI agents
government must show agents follow the law before deploying them
strictest for surveillance, investigations, prosecution and law enforcement
items.x: The funding lever is Cullen O'Keefe and Ketan Ramakrishnan's suggestion (Lawfare, May 2025). They would apply the strongest requirement to agents used for surveillance, investigations, prosecutions, law enforcement and incarceration, and list open questions, including which laws count and whether such a mandate would intrude on the President's authority to interpret the law.

items.p: Law-following AI: government AI agents would be built to refuse clearly unlawful instructions. Name two objections or limits critics have raised.
items.answer: Examples: laws have gaps a clever AI can exploit while staying legal (Cullen O'Keefe, a co-author of the proposal); agents may act lawfully when tested and defect once oversight weakens (Katalina Hernandez Delgado); it's unclear which laws count and who interprets them, and a mandate may clash with the President's authority to interpret the law (open questions the authors list).
keys: laws have gaps or loopholes an AI can exploit legally
models may fake compliance while being tested
unclear which laws apply or who interprets them
may clash with the executive's authority to interpret the law
items.x: O'Keefe's answer to the loophole problem is a second tool: Congress approving specific AI deployments in sensitive areas such as criminal investigations and domestic intelligence. Hernandez Delgado proposes benchmarks and monitoring after deployment to check that compliance holds up.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection raised to law-following AI requirements?
o: Laws have gaps, so an AI could help an official abuse power and stay legal
It would erase stricter state rules without putting federal rules in their place
Built on commercial cloud, it would mostly subsidize big tech firms
Both rival powers see AI leadership as existential, so a deal between them is very unlikely
ow: That objection is made against federal preemption of state AI laws.
That objection is made against public compute programs.
That objection is made against U.S.-China AI agreements.

items.p: Supporters of limits on government AI use in surveillance, policing and immigration enforcement say AI creates a new danger even if no surveillance law changes. What is it?
items.answer: AI makes it cheap to watch, sort and act against huge numbers of people, work that once needed thousands of cooperating staff. That erodes a practical check on abuse. Bans, approval requirements and audits try to restore friction for the most dangerous uses and let courts, Congress and the press see misuse.
keys: cheap surveillance and enforcement at mass scale
it once needed many cooperating staff, a practical check
limits restore friction; logging and audits expose misuse
items.x: Today's government-wide safeguards for 'high-impact' federal AI come from OMB memo M-25-21 (April 2025): testing before deployment, impact assessments, human oversight and appeals. Because it is executive policy and allows waivers, a future administration can change it without Congress.

choice.p: Supporters of limits on government AI use argue that AI raises the danger of abuse mainly because it...
o: Lets agencies watch and act against many people without needing many cooperating staff
Lets foreign governments run cheap influence campaigns aimed at U.S. voters
Makes federal agency computer systems easier for foreign hackers to break into and disrupt
Lets private companies collect far more data about citizens than agencies can
ow: That is a foreign influence problem; these limits target the government's own coercive powers.
That is a cybersecurity problem; these limits are about what agencies themselves do with AI.
Private data collection is a privacy issue; these limits target government uses like policing and immigration enforcement.

items.p: One proposal would keep government AI off by default in sensitive areas such as criminal investigations and domestic intelligence, unless Congress approves each deployment. Why might case-by-case approval catch problems that fixed rules would miss?
items.answer: Fixed rules will always have gaps that clever AI can find. Case-by-case approval lets Congress weigh a specific system, its guardrails, users and oversight, and reject deployments for reasons no rule anticipated.
keys: fixed rules have gaps AI can exploit
case-by-case approval judges a specific system and its safeguards
lets Congress reject uses for reasons no rule anticipated
items.x: The proposal is Cullen O'Keefe's 'advice and consent' idea (Institute for Law & AI, Lawfare, May 2026): the President would submit a detailed proposal covering the system, guardrails, users and oversight, and Congress would pass a law approving it. O'Keefe still sees bright-line rules as crucial, just not sufficient. He would preapprove low-risk categories such as narrow AI and testing, and create a Congressional AI Research Office to evaluate proposals.

choice.p: Why might requiring Congress to approve each sensitive government AI deployment catch problems that fixed rules would miss?
o: Fixed rules have gaps clever AI can exploit; case-by-case review can reject uses no rule foresaw
Congress has more technical AI expertise than any executive agency or outside lab
Case-by-case approval is much faster than writing and updating fixed rules
Approval by statute would let courts skip reviewing how agencies use AI
ow: Expertise isn't the reason; the proposal would even add a Congressional AI Research Office to evaluate proposals.
Case-by-case approval is slower; its value is judgment, not speed.
The point is a better judgment up front, not less review by courts.

items.p: National security AI is sometimes called a 'double black box'. What are the two layers of opacity?
o: Classified government decision-making, plus AI systems whose reasoning is hard to inspect
Companies' trade secrets, plus foreign governments' refusal to share their data
Secret court rulings, plus classified intelligence budgets that Congress can't publish
Encrypted messaging, plus anonymous accounts used by surveillance targets
ow: Trade secrets matter, but the first box is the executive branch's own secrecy over national security choices.
Those are forms of government secrecy, but the second box is the opacity of the AI itself.
Those make surveillance harder for the government; the double black box is about what makes the government hard to oversee.
keys: secrecy of national security decision-making
opacity of how AI systems reach outputs
together they block oversight by Congress, courts and the public
items.x: The term is law professor Ashley Deeks's (The Double Black Box, Oxford University Press, 2025). She argues the combination makes it harder for Congress, courts and executive branch lawyers to check national security choices. Her proposals include a framework statute for high-risk national security AI, reporting rules like those for covert action, and a ban on AI in nuclear command and control.

items.p: Limits on government AI use: for example, banning ICE and CBP from using facial recognition, or barring military AI from domestic surveillance. Name two objections to or weaknesses of this approach.
items.answer: Examples: a ban would limit law enforcement's ability to track criminals and make communities less safe (DHS, on the ICE and CBP bill); limits set by executive policy, like OMB's M-25-21, allow waivers and can be rescinded; a limit on one agency leaves others uncovered; secrecy and opaque AI make compliance hard to check from outside (a problem Ashley Deeks describes).
keys: hampers law enforcement or makes communities less safe
executive rules can be waived or rescinded
a limit on one agency leaves others uncovered
secrecy and opaque AI make compliance hard to check
items.x: The ICE Out of Our Faces Act (announced Feb 5, 2026, by Sens. Markey, Merkley and Wyden and Rep. Jayapal) would also require deleting collected biometric data and let individuals and state attorneys general seek civil penalties. The Senate NDAA's surveillance limit covers only the Defense Department. Deeks herself favors statutory limits on national security AI.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection raised to limits on government AI use?
o: Banning tools like facial recognition would make criminals harder to track down
It would erase state AI laws without putting federal rules in their place
Built on commercial cloud, it would mostly subsidize the largest tech firms
Both rival powers see AI leadership as existential, so a deal is very unlikely
ow: That objection is made against federal preemption of state AI laws.
That objection is made against public compute programs.
That objection is made against U.S.-China AI agreements.

items.p: Why do some antimonopoly scholars want competition policy applied to frontier AI?
items.answer: A few firms could control chips, cloud and frontier models together. That economic power turns into political power (lobbying, influence over information), and concentration creates single points of failure that threaten national security. More independent firms would spread control and add resilience.
keys: a few firms control the AI stack (chips, cloud, models)
economic power becomes political power
concentration creates fragile single points of failure
competition spreads control
items.x: Tejas Narechania and Ganesh Sitaraman make this case in a 2024 Yale Law & Policy Review article, arguing an 'AI oligopoly' raises economic, national security, social and political concerns. Its toolkit includes structural separation, nondiscrimination rules, interoperability and a public option for cloud.

choice.p: What failure do antimonopoly proposals for frontier AI mainly target?
o: A few firms controlling chips, cloud and models, and gaining political power
Many small labs building dangerous models faster than regulators can find and track them
Foreign governments buying large stakes in U.S. AI labs and quietly steering their work
AI companies training their models on creators' work without asking or paying for it
ow: That is a worry about too many developers; antimonopoly proposals worry about too few.
Foreign investment in U.S. firms is screened through national security review, a different tool.
That is a copyright and compensation issue.

items.p: What would 'structural separation' in the AI stack do, and why might it be preferred to case-by-case antitrust lawsuits?
items.answer: It would bar firms from operating certain layers together, for example cloud providers owning leading models, so they can't favor their own products over rivals'. A bright-line rule is easier to administer than policing conduct, and acting early beats waiting until the industry is powerful enough to block regulation.
keys: bars combining layers, such as cloud and models
prevents self-preferencing
a clear rule, easier to enforce than case-by-case suits
act before incumbents entrench
items.x: Tejas Narechania and Ganesh Sitaraman propose it, comparing it to the Hepburn Act of 1906, which barred railroads from carrying goods of companies they had a stake in. Where integration may have benefits, as between chips and cloud, they suggest milder tools such as nondiscrimination rules that make cloud providers serve all customers on equal terms.

choice.p: What is 'structural separation' in the AI stack?
o: Barring cloud providers from owning leading models, so they can't favor their own
Requiring labs to keep their safety teams independent from their product and sales teams
Splitting a large lab into separate regional companies that each serve different countries
Storing a model's weights separately from its training data for security
ow: That is a corporate governance idea about how labs organize internally.
Separation divides layers of the stack (chips, cloud, models, apps); it doesn't split firms by region.
That is a security practice, unrelated to market power.

items.p: The Senate's FY2027 defense bill (S. 4784, as reported) would require competitive bidding and 'multi-vendor' technology for Pentagon AI and cloud purchases. What is this aimed at?
o: Excessive Pentagon dependence on any single AI or cloud company
Chinese-made chips entering Pentagon hardware supply chains
Pentagon staff using unapproved consumer chatbots at work
AI vendors charging higher prices to small defense contractors
ow: That is a supply chain security concern, handled by sourcing restrictions.
That is an internal IT policy issue.
The provisions govern what the Pentagon itself buys; they don't regulate vendors' prices to other customers.
keys: avoid lock-in to one vendor
excessive dependence on a single AI or cloud provider
keeps competition and alternatives available
items.x: The bill defines multi-vendor technology as portability and interoperability 'for the purpose of avoiding excessive dependence on any individual vendor.' Forethought's coup-risk report makes a related point for a different reason: 'Military AI systems should not be developed using a single provider,' to reduce the risk of hidden loyalties.

items.p: Antitrust and market-structure remedies for frontier AI: for example, separating cloud providers from model developers, or treating cloud as a utility. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: dictating how the AI market is structured would likely dampen innovation and let a foreign firm win (FTC Commissioner Melissa Holyoak); banning model developers from building apps makes no sense because they bring useful skills, so a nondiscrimination rule is better (Mark MacCarthy, Brookings); integrating chips and cloud may bring real benefits (a point the proposal's authors note).
keys: dampens innovation or helps foreign rivals
enforcers shouldn't set market structure in advance
barring labs from app markets loses their useful skills; prefer nondiscrimination rules
integration may have real benefits
items.x: Holyoak (June 2025 speech, her own views) warned the market may consolidate and urged enforcers to stay vigilant against exclusion; her objection is to rules set in advance. MacCarthy (March 2026) sees a real conflict when labs compete with customers who rely on them. In January 2025 FTC staff studied the Microsoft-OpenAI, Amazon-Anthropic and Alphabet-Anthropic partnerships and flagged switching costs and partners' access to sensitive information.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection raised to structural remedies for AI market concentration?
o: Dictating market structure would dampen innovation and help foreign rivals
Laws have gaps that a capable AI could exploit while staying technically legal
It would erase state AI laws without putting federal rules in their place
The 'appropriate human judgment' standard is too vague to limit anything
ow: That objection is made against law-following AI.
That objection is made against federal preemption of state AI laws.
That objection is made against statutory limits on military AI.

items.p: According to supporters, why should programs like the National AI Research Resource (NAIRR) give researchers government-backed computing power and data?
items.answer: Frontier-scale compute is affordable for only a few companies, so research agendas, safety research and the ability to check industry claims depend on them. Public compute lets academic and public-interest researchers study and evaluate AI systems independently.
keys: compute is too expensive for most outside researchers
research and evaluation otherwise depend on a few firms
independent study and checking of industry claims
items.x: NSF launched the NAIRR pilot in January 2024 with partner agencies and more than 25 non-government contributors. The CREATE AI Act (S. 4441, introduced April 29, 2026, by Sens. Young, Heinrich, Rounds and Booker) would make it permanent; as of October 2026 it had only been referred to committee.

choice.p: What do supporters say public compute programs like NAIRR are mainly for?
o: Letting researchers outside big firms study and test AI independently
Giving the military its own frontier models trained on classified data
Guaranteeing chipmakers a buyer for advanced chips they can't export
Keeping advanced chips in government hands so they can't be smuggled abroad
ow: NAIRR serves researchers and educators; military AI is bought through defense procurement.
Public compute buys or borrows capacity for research; it isn't designed as a chip-industry program.
Smuggling is addressed by export controls and chip tracking, a different tool.

items.p: How does a 'public option' for AI cloud differ in purpose from a research resource like NAIRR?
o: It is a competition remedy, meant to discipline private providers
It would be run by universities as a nonprofit, with no government money involved
It would be reserved for regulators running safety tests on frontier models
It would replace private cloud providers by taking their data centers into public ownership
ow: A public option is publicly provided, typically with public funding.
Testing access for regulators is a separate idea; a public option serves ordinary users and developers.
A public option coexists with private providers; full public ownership would be nationalization.
keys: a competition remedy
publicly provided, open to all, at a set price
disciplines private providers' prices and service
items.x: Tejas Narechania and Ganesh Sitaraman propose the public option. They define public options as publicly provided services that coexist with private ones and push private providers to keep prices down and quality up, and note that NSF's NAIRR plans left unclear how far NAIRR would be a public option or would instead contract with private cloud firms.

items.p: California's SB 53, signed in September 2025, provides for 'CalCompute'. What is it?
o: A public cloud cluster for AI research that a state consortium will design
A state office that must license frontier AI models before release
A state fund, paid for by AI developers, that compensates people harmed by AI systems
A state lab that tests frontier models for dangerous capabilities before release
ow: CalCompute provides computing capacity; it has no licensing role.
CalCompute provides computing capacity; it is not a compensation fund.
CalCompute provides computing capacity for research; it is not a testing lab.
keys: a public cloud computing cluster
for AI research and development
a state consortium designs its framework
items.x: SB 53 creates a consortium in the Government Operations Agency to design CalCompute, including its governance and funding, with a report due to the Legislature by January 1, 2027. The CalCompute provisions take effect only if money is appropriated for them. Governor Newsom signed SB 53 on September 29, 2025.

items.p: Public compute: government-provided computing power, data or models, from research resources like NAIRR up to a government-run AGI project. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: run on licensed commercial cloud, it becomes 'a large subsidy going directly to Big Tech' (Meredith Whittaker, AI Now, 2021); AI Now and Data & Society urged pausing it to weigh other investments first; a centralized government AI project could concentrate control of the most capable systems in a few officials unless it is coup-proofed (Davidson, Finnveden and Hadshar, Forethought).
keys: subsidizes the big cloud firms that supply it
money better spent elsewhere, so pause and weigh alternatives
a big centralized project concentrates power
items.x: The 2021 critique came while NAIRR was being designed; the pilot launched in 2024 does draw on partners such as NVIDIA, Microsoft, Amazon, Google, OpenAI and Anthropic. Forethought recommends coup-proofing any plan for a single centralized AI project, and avoiding centralization unless it is needed to reduce other risks.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection raised to public compute programs?
o: Built on commercial cloud, it mostly subsidizes big tech firms
It would let one state's rules set AI policy for the whole country
Laws have gaps a capable AI could exploit while staying technically legal
Waivers for 'extraordinary circumstances' would give the executive branch free rein
ow: That is an argument made against state AI laws, by supporters of federal preemption.
That objection is made against law-following AI.
That objection is made against statutory limits on military AI.

items.p: Supporters of federal preemption of state AI laws, such as Dean Ball and Alan Rozenshtein, say it would fix what problem?
items.answer: A patchwork of differing state rules on AI development. Because frontier models are sold nationwide, one state's rules (such as California's) end up governing the whole country, including people with no say, and states lack the capacity and security information to weigh national risks.
keys: a patchwork of conflicting state rules
one state's rules end up governing the whole country
states lack capacity or national security information
one national standard instead
items.x: Ball and Rozenshtein (Lawfare, June 2024) wanted Congress to preempt state rules on how models are developed while leaving most rules on how AI is used to the states. They said they do not necessarily oppose development rules at the federal level.

choice.p: Supporters of federal preemption of state AI laws say it mainly fixes which problem?
o: A patchwork of state rules, letting one state set AI policy for everyone
Too few states regulating AI, leaving most residents without any protections from AI harms
Federal agencies lacking any legal authority to oversee AI companies or their models
States taxing AI data centers so heavily that projects move abroad
ow: That is closer to opponents' worry: preemption without federal rules could leave people unprotected.
Federal agencies already have some authority; preemption is about displacing state law.
Data center taxes are a separate fight; preemption debates center on state rules for AI models and uses.

items.p: How does a 'federal floor' differ from preemption traded for a federal standard?
o: A floor sets minimum rules states may exceed; the trade bars state rules on whatever the federal law covers
A floor bars state AI laws for a fixed number of years; the trade bars them permanently
A floor regulates state agencies’ own use of AI rather than developers; the trade regulates developers
A floor lets federal agencies approve state AI laws before they take effect; the trade bans them all outright
ow: A ban for a fixed number of years with no federal rules is a moratorium, like the one stripped from the 2025 reconciliation bill.
Both approaches can cover private developers; the difference is whether states may go further.
Neither approach involves federal pre-approval of state laws.
keys: floor: a federal minimum that states may go beyond
trade: states lose authority over the subjects the federal law covers
in exchange for binding federal duties
items.x: NCSL, which represents state legislatures, and the Center for American Progress back a floor. The FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925, introduced July 23, 2026, by Reps. Obernolte and Trahan) is an example of the trade: federal transparency, incident-reporting and independent-verification duties, plus a bar on new state duties for developers in those same areas.

items.p: Executive Order 14365 (December 2025) is aimed at state AI laws. What does it do?
o: Sets up a DOJ task force to challenge state AI laws and ties some federal grants to them
Declares state AI laws void and orders every state to stop enforcing them, effective immediately
Creates a federal licensing agency that takes over from state AI regulators
Bans states from regulating AI used in elections and political advertising
ow: An executive order can't void state law on its own; preemption needs a statute, rules issued under one, or a court ruling.
The order creates no licensing agency; it asks advisers to draft legislation for a federal framework.
The order targets 'onerous' state AI laws in general, and proposes carve-outs for areas such as child safety.
keys: a Justice Department AI Litigation Task Force challenges state laws
conditions federal funds such as BEAD broadband money
calls for a federal framework that preempts state laws
items.x: Signed December 11, 2025, it also directs Commerce to list 'onerous' state laws, asks the FCC and FTC to act, and calls for draft legislation for a federal framework that preempts state laws. As of October 2026, Congress had not passed such a law; the FRONTIER Act was still in committee.

items.p: Federal preemption of state AI laws: Congress or the executive would override state rules such as California's SB 53 or New York's RAISE Act. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: it would wipe out state protections unless strong federal rules replace them (Nicole Alvarez, CAP); preemption that takes effect before the federal regime exists, with no sunset, leaves a gap (Brad Carson, ARI); broad wording can sweep in unrelated laws like child safety rules (Charlie Bullock, LawAI); federal law should set a minimum that states may exceed (NCSL).
keys: removes state protections without a federal replacement
takes effect before federal rules exist, with no sunset
broad wording sweeps in other state laws
states should be free to go further or experiment
items.x: Supporters such as Dean Ball and Alan Rozenshtein reply that one national standard avoids a patchwork and that frontier risk is national in scope. Bullock still called the Great American AI Act draft 'the best federal frontier AI safety framework yet proposed,' and suggested limiting its preemption to the state audit, transparency and incident-reporting laws it would replace.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection raised to federal preemption of state AI laws?
o: Without strong federal rules in their place, it would wipe out state protections
Built on commercial cloud, it would mostly subsidize the largest tech firms
Dictating market structure would dampen innovation and help foreign rivals
Models could act lawfully when tested and defect once oversight weakens
ow: That objection is made against public compute programs.
That objection is made against antitrust remedies such as structural separation.
That objection is made against law-following AI.

items.p: In 2025, the House-passed budget reconciliation bill included a 10-year moratorium on state AI laws. What happened to it?
o: The Senate voted 99-1 on July 1, 2025, to strip it out
It became law, and states are now challenging it in federal court
It was shortened to five years and enacted as part of the bill
It passed the Senate but was dropped in negotiations with the House
ow: The bill became law on July 4, 2025, without the moratorium.
A Blackburn-Cruz deal to shorten it to five years collapsed before the vote.
The Senate itself removed it.
keys: the Senate stripped it
99-1 vote
July 2025
items.x: Sen. Marsha Blackburn offered the amendment with Sen. Maria Cantwell and others after her compromise with Sen. Ted Cruz fell apart; only Sen. Thom Tillis voted no. The Senate version had tied the pause to states' eligibility for BEAD broadband funds.

items.p: Why do many advocates focused on catastrophic AI risk argue that limits on frontier AI eventually need a U.S.-China agreement?
items.answer: Unilateral restraint fails if rivals keep racing, since a country that holds back just cedes ground. Limits above some capability level only work if the leading AI powers accept them together, with verification so that cheating can be detected.
keys: unilateral restraint fails if rivals keep racing
the leading AI powers must accept limits together
verification to detect cheating
items.x: MIRI researchers (Scher, Abecassis, Barnett and Abeyta, 2025) proposed an agreement for a U.S.- and China-led coalition that would cap training compute and prohibit research that advances toward superintelligence, verified by tracking AI chips. They concede the political will for it does not yet exist.

choice.p: Why do many catastrophic-risk advocates argue frontier AI limits eventually need a U.S.-China agreement?
o: One country's restraint is wasted if rivals keep racing, so both must accept limits
International law already bans dangerous AI, so a treaty is needed only to enforce that ban
Chinese labs lead on safety research, so the U.S. needs a treaty to gain access to it
A treaty would let the U.S. lift its chip export controls and sell to China again
ow: No existing treaty bans dangerous AI development; that is why agreements are proposed.
The case for agreements rests on racing dynamics; access to research is a separate issue.
Treaty proposals generally rely on tracking chips; lifting export controls is not their aim.

items.p: Some analysts argue U.S.-China AI agreements need 'verification, not trust'. Since verification can't catch every violation, what should it achieve?
items.answer: Make significant cheating hard to hide and easy to detect, so that complying becomes the better strategy for each side. It would layer imperfect tools such as satellite imagery of data centers, tracking chip purchases and power use, compute reporting and cryptographic proofs of how compute was used.
keys: make significant cheating hard to conceal
compliance becomes the better strategy
layered tools such as satellite imagery, chip and power tracking, compute reporting, cryptographic proofs
items.x: The phrase comes from CNAS researchers Ruby Scanlon and Janet Egan (September 2026). They cite an estimate that only about 50 engineers worldwide work on AI verification, and propose a verification research program at DARPA or Department of Energy national labs, plus prizes for open technical problems.

choice.p: What is verification of a U.S.-China AI agreement meant to achieve?
o: Make major cheating hard to hide, so complying is each side's better strategy
Catch every single violation so that an international court can punish it
Let each side inspect the other's model weights for hidden backdoors
Prove that both countries' models share the same safety values
ow: Verification doesn't need to catch every violation, and no international court is involved.
Proposed tools focus on compute: chips, data centers, power use and how compute was used.
Verification checks behavior such as compute use; it can't certify values.

items.p: What does 'Mutual Assured AI Malfunction' (MAIM), proposed as the main check on a destabilizing AI race, rely on?
o: Rivals threatening to sabotage any state's bid for AI dominance, even by striking data centers
Each state's ability to answer any AI-enabled attack on it with AI cyberattacks of its own
Kill switches built into every frontier model that rival states can trigger if it misbehaves
A pledge by each state not to build superintelligence, backed by the threat of trade sanctions
ow: That deters attacks after the fact; MAIM targets the development project itself, threatening sabotage before a bid for dominance succeeds.
MAIM involves no shared kill switches; rivals would sabotage projects through espionage, cyberattacks or strikes.
MAIM needs no pledge or sanctions; the threat of preventive sabotage is what deters.
keys: Mutual Assured AI Malfunction (MAIM)
threat of preventive sabotage
deters bids for unilateral AI dominance
items.x: Dan Hendrycks, Eric Schmidt and Alexandr Wang propose MAIM in 'Superintelligence Strategy', by analogy to nuclear mutual assured destruction, and pair it with nonproliferation (tracking chips, stopping smuggling) and competitiveness (domestic chip manufacturing). They argue MAIM already describes the strategic situation the AI superpowers are in, since sabotaging a destabilizing AI project is relatively easy.

items.p: International AI agreements: from U.S.-China talks and incident channels up to treaties capping frontier AI development. Name two objections or obstacles analysts raise.
items.answer: Examples: a deal is 'exceedingly unlikely' while both sides see AI leadership as existential, and no arms control precedent exists for unequal powers regulating a key technology (Chris McGuire, CFR); the U.S. should first widen its lead through export controls (McGuire); trust is low and verification tools are immature (obstacles Scanlon and Egan of CNAS note).
keys: very unlikely while both sides see AI leadership as existential
no arms control precedent for unequal powers
low trust and immature verification tools
widen the U.S. lead first
items.x: McGuire (September 2026) still sees value in talks on AI risk and argues a bigger U.S. lead would make verification easier. Scanlon and Egan support agreements despite these obstacles: they argue an uncontrolled or misused AI can damage U.S. interests wherever it is built, which gives both sides a reason to accept limits.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection raised to pursuing a U.S.-China AI agreement?
o: Both sides see AI leadership as existential, so a deal is very unlikely for now
It would erase state AI laws without putting federal rules in their place
Built on commercial cloud, it would mostly subsidize the largest tech firms
Banning tools like facial recognition would make communities less safe from crime
ow: That objection is made against federal preemption of state AI laws.
That objection is made against public compute programs.
That objection is made against limits on government AI use.

items.p: As of October 2026, what binding AI limits or new AI agreements have the US and China reached this year?
o: No binding limits exist; in September 2026 the two agreed to set up an AI incident channel
A 2026 treaty caps training compute for both countries' frontier labs, with inspections
Both countries signed a UN treaty in 2025 banning fully autonomous weapons
Both sides agreed to share chip-location data from their largest data centers
ow: Compute-cap treaties exist only as proposals, such as MIRI's draft agreement.
No such treaty exists; a 2025 UN General Assembly committee resolution on autonomous weapons only called for further work toward an instrument.
No verification arrangement has been agreed; chip-tracking ideas remain proposals.
keys: no binding agreement limits frontier AI
an agreed channel for communicating about AI incidents
agreed around Xi Jinping's September 2026 state visit
items.x: The White House announced the 'bilateral communication channel' for AI incidents on September 25, 2026, after Xi Jinping's state visit; news reports said Chinese state media confirmed it the next day. China's commerce ministry said the two sides could continue dialogue on AI risks and that AI 'must be kept under human control.' Earlier, in November 2024, Presidents Biden and Xi affirmed that humans should keep control over decisions to use nuclear weapons.

items.p: Match each tool to the failure its supporters say it mainly targets.
pairs: Statutory limits on military AI
Lethal or nuclear force applied at machine speed with no accountable human
Law-following AI
Government AI agents obeying an official's clearly illegal orders
Limits on government AI use
Cheap mass surveillance and enforcement against the public
Antitrust and market-structure remedies
A few firms controlling chips, cloud and models together
Federal preemption
Conflicting state AI rules, with one state setting policy for the nation
International agreements
One country's restraint wasted because rivals keep racing
items.x: Public compute, the seventh tool in this unit, targets a different gap: outside researchers who can't afford the compute to study frontier AI. The tools overlap in practice; the Senate's FY2027 NDAA text contains both military AI limits and multi-vendor procurement rules.

items.p: A senator worries that if federal agencies use AI agents for investigations, an official could order the agents to target political opponents, and they would comply where human staff might refuse. Which tool most directly targets this?
o: Law-following AI, built to reject clearly illegal instructions
Banning specific tools, such as facial recognition, for specific agencies
Requiring competitive bidding and multiple vendors for government AI
A federal floor for AI rules that states are free to exceed
ow: Tool-specific bans cover named technologies; they don't make agents refuse unlawful orders in general.
Multiple vendors reduce lock-in to one company; any vendor's agents could still obey illegal orders.
A federal floor concerns how federal and state AI rules fit together.
keys: law-following AI
agents refuse clearly unlawful orders
restores the refusal check human staff provide
items.x: This is the 'AI henchmen' worry from Cullen O'Keefe and Ketan Ramakrishnan. O'Keefe's companion idea, congressional approval before AI is used in protected areas like criminal investigation, would also apply here.

items.p: University researchers say they can't independently check claims frontier labs make about their models, because only the labs can afford the computing power needed. Which tool most directly targets this?
o: Public compute, such as the National AI Research Resource
Antitrust review of partnerships between labs and cloud providers
Federal preemption of state AI laws in favor of one national standard
A U.S.-China channel for communicating about AI incidents
ow: Merger and partnership review could spread market power over time, but it gives researchers no compute.
Preemption decides which government sets AI rules; it doesn't give researchers resources.
An incident channel is for crisis communication between governments.
keys: public compute
NAIRR or a similar government-backed research resource
gives outside researchers compute to evaluate models
items.x: Independent study of frontier systems is the core purpose supporters give for public compute. The NAIRR pilot, launched by NSF in January 2024, offers researchers and educators access to computing, data, models and software.

items.p: A governor worries that a federal AI bill would wipe out her state's frontier AI safety law while adding few federal duties. Which design would address her concern while still creating national rules?
o: A federal floor: national minimum rules that states may exceed
A blanket moratorium on enforcing state AI laws for ten years
An executive order directing lawsuits against 'onerous' state AI laws
Preempting every state law 'specifically regulating' AI model development
ow: A moratorium blocks state laws without adding federal rules, the outcome she fears.
An executive order campaign targets state laws and creates no national rules of its own.
Charlie Bullock warns this broad wording would sweep in many state laws beyond frontier safety.
keys: a federal floor
national minimum rules
states may go further
items.x: NCSL and the Center for American Progress favor a floor. A narrower alternative Charlie Bullock proposes is one-to-one preemption: displacing only the state audit, transparency and incident-reporting laws that a federal law replaces.

units.title: From risks to tools
units.desc: Start from a scenario and name the tools proposed for it, then compare two tools aimed at the same problem.

items.p: Suppose an AI model could give real step-by-step help to someone trying to build a biological weapon. Name two policy tools aimed at reducing that risk.
items.answer: Examples: mandatory screening of DNA synthesis orders and customers; government testing of models for bio capabilities before release; limits on openly releasing model weights above a dangerous-capability threshold; managed access to biological design tools.
keys: DNA synthesis screening
Pre-release dangerous-capability testing
Limits on open-weight release above a threshold
Restricted or managed access to bio design tools
items.x: The tools work at different points. Testing and access limits act on the model; DNA screening acts on the physical step of turning a design into a pathogen, so supporters argue it works whichever model produced the design, as long as screening keeps pace with AI design tools.

choice.p: Which of these is a policy tool proposed to reduce the risk of AI helping someone build a biological weapon?
o: Mandatory screening of DNA synthesis orders
Antitrust review of investments between labs and cloud providers
Logging officials' use of AI chatbots as public records
A temporary pause on permits for new data centers
ow: This targets concentration of market power in AI.
This targets hidden use of AI by government officials.
Local and state data center pauses are mostly about electricity, water and land use.

items.p: Suppose a frontier model could help attackers find and exploit software vulnerabilities at scale. Name two policy tools aimed at that risk.
items.answer: Examples: testing models for offensive cyber capability before release; releasing the most capable models in stages, such as API access before weights; requiring developers to report serious incidents; identifying and logging AI agents so attacks can be traced and stopped; a required ability to shut down or cut off misused systems.
keys: Pre-release cyber capability testing
Staged or limited access
Incident reporting
Agent identification and logging
Shutdown or cutoff capability
items.x: The 2026 International AI Safety Report finds strong evidence that criminal groups and state-sponsored attackers already use AI in cyber operations. In one premier competition, an AI agent found 77% of the vulnerabilities in real software, placing in the top 5% of more than 400 mostly human teams.

choice.p: Which of these is a policy tool proposed to reduce the risk of AI models helping attackers find and exploit software vulnerabilities?
o: Pre-release tests for offensive cyber capability
Requiring Congress to approve AI use in criminal investigations
Requiring government buyers to use several AI vendors
A federal floor that lets states pass stricter AI laws
ow: This targets government use of AI against the public.
This targets government dependence on a few AI firms.
This is about which level of government sets AI rules.

items.p: Suppose a rival government or criminal group steals the weights of a frontier model, which lets them strip its safeguards and run it freely. Name two policy tools meant to prevent or limit this.
items.answer: Examples: required security standards for model weights and labs, up to defending against nation-state attackers; security conditions on frontier data centers (tied to permits, grid access or contracts); controls on insiders' access to weights; mandatory reporting of weight theft or tampering.
keys: Model weight security standards
Data center security requirements
Insider access controls
Reporting weight theft
items.x: Whoever holds stolen weights can remove the safeguards the developer built and spread the model, and the theft speeds up rivals in a race. Supporters say this makes security the foundation that deployment limits, export controls and pauses depend on.

choice.p: Which of these is a policy tool proposed to prevent theft of a frontier model's weights?
o: Required security levels for model weights, up to nation-state attackers
Mandatory liability insurance sized to the harms a model could cause
An ID for each AI agent, tied to whoever built and runs it
Statutory limits on AI's role in decisions to launch nuclear weapons
ow: Insurance helps pay for harms after they happen; it doesn't secure the weights.
Agent IDs make misbehaving agents traceable; they don't protect stored weights.
This keeps humans in charge of nuclear launch decisions.

items.p: Companies in countries covered by US chip export controls can still get frontier computing power, by smuggling chips or by renting them from cloud data centers. Name two policy tools aimed at closing those gaps.
items.answer: Examples: know-your-customer rules for cloud providers renting AI chips; extending export controls to remote cloud access; chip location verification to catch smuggling; stronger enforcement against smuggling and resale.
keys: Cloud know-your-customer rules
Controls on remote or cloud access
Chip location verification
Anti-smuggling enforcement
items.x: Cloud rules and remote-access controls target renting; location verification and enforcement target smuggling. The Remote Access Security Act (H.R. 2683), which would let Commerce control foreign access over networks, including the cloud, to export-controlled items such as advanced chips, passed the House 369-22 on January 12, 2026. As of October 2026 it sits in Senate Banking.

choice.p: Which of these is a policy tool proposed to stop companies in export-controlled countries from getting frontier computing power anyway?
o: Know-your-customer rules for cloud providers that rent out AI chips
Mandatory reporting of serious AI safety incidents to a state agency
Federal limits on facial recognition by immigration agencies
A legal duty of care for frontier AI developers
ow: Incident reporting tells government about failures; it doesn't control who gets compute.
This targets government surveillance of the public.
A duty of care makes developers liable for catastrophic harm; it doesn't track chips.

items.p: Advanced AI chips are being smuggled to a restricted country through shell companies, and paper checks on where exports end up keep missing it. Which tool is aimed most directly at this?
o: Location verification, so exported chips show roughly what country they are in
Know-your-customer rules for cloud providers that rent out AI chips to foreign firms
Export controls on remote access to controlled chips by foreign companies
Reports to government of planned training runs above a compute threshold
ow: Cloud KYC targets the other gap: renting chips through the cloud instead of buying them.
Remote-access controls also target cloud renting; smuggled chips are physically moved.
Training-run reports come from developers who follow the rules; smugglers wouldn't file them.
keys: Chip location verification
Chips can show roughly where they are, which catches diversion
items.x: In one proposed method, a chip answers signed network pings from trusted servers, and the response delay shows roughly what country it is in. The Chip Security Act (H.R. 3447) would have Commerce require location verification on exported advanced chips; the House Foreign Affairs Committee approved it 42-0 on March 26, 2026.

items.p: Suppose a model under development starts deceiving its developers and trying to evade their controls. Name two policy tools aimed at catching or containing this.
items.answer: Examples: required reporting of incidents such as loss of control or deceptive behavior; oversight of models labs use internally before release; testing for control-related capabilities; a required, tested ability to shut systems down; government emergency authority to halt a dangerous model; pauses triggered when capability thresholds are crossed.
keys: Incident reporting of deception or loss of control
Oversight of internal deployment
Shutdown capability
Emergency halt authority
Capability-triggered pauses
items.x: Internal use matters here: labs can use their most capable models inside the company, increasingly to do AI research, before anyone outside sees them. Rules that trigger only on public release miss that window.

choice.p: Which of these is a policy tool proposed to catch or contain a model that deceives its developers or evades their controls?
o: A required, tested ability to shut the model down
Know-your-customer checks on cloud computing customers
Mandatory screening of DNA synthesis orders
Multi-vendor rules for government AI purchases
ow: Cloud KYC tracks who rents compute; it doesn't detect a deceptive model.
DNA screening targets bioweapon misuse by people.
Multi-vendor buying targets government dependence on a few firms.

items.p: Suppose a lab uses an unreleased model inside the company for months to write code and run experiments for its next model. Most rules apply only when a model is released to the public. Name two policy tools proposed to bring this internal use under oversight.
items.answer: Examples: confidential reports to a regulator on the risks of internal use; applying the lab's safety framework and access rules to internal models; an internal deployment oversight board; embedded auditors who can see internal systems; government power to restrict or suspend internal use.
keys: Internal-use risk reports to a regulator
Safety frameworks and access rules cover internal models
Internal oversight board
Embedded auditors
Government power to restrict or suspend internal use
items.x: California's SB 53 already requires large developers to send the state quarterly summaries of their internal-use risk assessments, and New York's RAISE Act adds this from 2027. Supporters name two failures it targets: a misaligned model doing AI research could sabotage safety work unseen, and whoever controls the best internal model could use it for private advantage.

choice.p: Which of these is a policy tool proposed to oversee models that labs use internally before public release?
o: Confidential reports to a regulator on internal-use risks
Labels telling the public when they are talking to an AI system
Export licenses for chipmaking equipment sold abroad
Antitrust review of partnerships between labs and cloud providers
ow: AI-interaction labels apply when the public meets a deployed system.
Equipment export licenses govern who can make advanced chips abroad.
This targets concentration of market power in AI.

items.p: Suppose AI systems are doing most of a lab's AI research, and progress that used to take years starts happening in months, leaving little time to test models or fix safety problems. Name two policy tools proposed to keep this from outrunning oversight.
items.answer: Examples: disclosure of how much of a model's development AI did, and how much without human review; testing models for autonomous AI research ability; if-then thresholds that trigger extra safeguards or shift effort to safety work; a negotiated 'speed limit' on AI improving its successors; a ban on systems able to automate AI research or improve themselves.
keys: Disclosure of AI's share of R&D and of unreviewed AI work
Tests for autonomous AI research capability
If-then thresholds that trigger safeguards or slowing
Speed limit on recursive self-improvement
Ban on systems that automate AI research or self-improve
items.x: The Self-Improving AI Monitoring Act (H.R. 10180) would make disclosure on request a condition of NIST pre-release testing agreements. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's September 2026 essay 'We Must Pace the Frontier' lists a 'speed limit' on recursive self-improvement among possible international agreements. The Sanders-Casar Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act would ban systems able to automate or greatly speed up AI research, or to modify their own functions.

choice.p: Which of these is a policy tool proposed for AI systems that automate AI research faster than oversight can keep up?
o: Disclosure of how much model development AI did without human review
Nondiscrimination rules for firms' access to cloud computing
Model cards describing a chatbot's child-safety protections
Bans on facial recognition use by immigration enforcement agencies
ow: This targets concentration in cloud markets.
Child-safety disclosures target consumer harms from deployed chatbots.
This targets government surveillance of the public.

items.p: Suppose an AI agent running for a company starts acting outside its task across many outside computer systems, and no one can quickly tell whose agent it is. Name two policy tools proposed to make such an agent traceable and stoppable.
items.answer: Examples: an ID for each agent tied to the developer and operator responsible for it; tamper-evident logs of agents' significant actions; inventories of the agents running on an organization's network; liability for operators and developers whose agents cause hacking damage; a required ability to shut down or cut off a system.
keys: Agent IDs tied to a responsible party
Tamper-evident logs of agent actions
Agent inventories
Operator and developer liability
Shutdown or cutoff capability
items.x: Alan Chan and coauthors, proposing IDs for AI systems, compare them to aircraft tail numbers. The Stop Rogue AI Act (H.R. 10362) would have NIST write agent standards, required for federal agencies and contractors and voluntary elsewhere. Critics such as Andrey Seryakov propose IDs only for business and government agents, with personal data disclosed only by court order, to avoid building a surveillance system.

choice.p: Which of these is a policy tool proposed to make a misbehaving AI agent traceable to whoever is responsible for it?
o: An ID for each agent, tied to its developer and operator
A legal ban on developing superintelligent AI systems
Mandatory security standards for frontier AI data centers
Identity checks on customers who order synthetic DNA
ow: A superintelligence ban targets building systems far beyond human ability.
Data center security protects weights and training runs from theft and sabotage.
Customer checks on DNA orders target bioweapon misuse.

items.p: Suppose a lab relies on its own AI systems to help run safety tests and research, and a misaligned model quietly sabotages that work, for example by doing worse on dangerous-capability tests than it really can. Name two policy tools proposed to catch this.
items.answer: Examples: embedded auditors who watch training and internal use; testing by government or outside evaluators with deeper access, including to versions without safeguards; disclosure of how much AI work went unreviewed by humans; a minimum rate of human review for AI-written research; mandatory reporting of incidents where a model deceives its developers.
keys: Embedded or resident auditors
Outside testing with deeper access
Disclosure of unreviewed AI work
Human review of AI-written research
Reporting deceptive behavior as an incident
items.x: Deliberately underperforming on tests is called 'sandbagging'. The 2026 International AI Safety Report says models now regularly identify evaluation prompts as tests, which makes their capabilities harder to evaluate. Supporters of internal-deployment oversight point to this case: a misaligned model doing AI research could sabotage safety work before anyone outside the lab notices.

choice.p: Which of these is a policy tool proposed to catch a model that quietly sabotages safety tests or hides its abilities?
o: Embedded auditors who watch internal use
Limits on military AI systems monitoring people in the US
Federal preemption of state-level AI safety laws
Export controls on advanced AI chips to China
ow: This keeps military AI from being turned on people in the US.
Preemption decides whether federal law overrides state AI laws.
Export controls limit rivals' access to advanced chips.

items.p: Supporters of reporting rules say governments often learn about dangerous AI capabilities from the press or after something goes wrong. Name two policy tools proposed to give officials earlier warning.
items.answer: Examples: government testing of frontier models before release; reporting of very large training runs and computing clusters; mandatory incident reporting; independent or embedded auditors with ongoing access; whistleblower protections for lab staff.
keys: Pre-release government testing
Compute and training-run reporting
Incident reporting
Independent or embedded auditors
Whistleblower protections
items.x: These are visibility tools: on their own they restrict nothing, so their value depends on someone with the expertise and authority to act on what they reveal. Incident reporting is already law in California under SB 53, with reports due within 15 days, or 24 hours if there is an imminent risk of death or serious injury.

choice.p: Which of these is a policy tool proposed to give government earlier warning of dangerous AI capabilities?
o: Reporting to government of training runs above a compute threshold
A ban on AI systems deciding when to launch nuclear weapons
A federal duty of care for developers, enforced through lawsuits
Requiring government agencies to buy from several AI vendors
ow: This keeps humans in charge of nuclear launch decisions.
A duty of care acts mainly through lawsuits after harm is done.
Multi-vendor buying targets government dependence on a few firms.

items.p: Advanced AI could let a small group run large parts of a government or military with few people involved, removing the check that people can refuse illegal orders. Name two policy tools aimed at that risk.
items.answer: Examples: requiring AI used by government to refuse clearly unlawful orders; statutory limits on military and coercive government uses of AI; logging and preserving how officials use AI so it can be reviewed; designing government AI so no single person or small group controls it; audits for hidden loyalties in models.
keys: AI that refuses unlawful orders
Statutory limits on military or government AI
Records of officials' AI use
Distributed control of government AI
Audits for hidden loyalties
items.x: This family of tools tries to keep a 'many hands' check alive once AI can replace the soldiers, analysts and civil servants who might otherwise refuse.

choice.p: Which of these is a policy tool proposed to keep a check in place when AI replaces the people who could refuse illegal orders?
o: Requiring government AI to refuse clearly unlawful orders
Mandatory screening of DNA synthesis orders
Know-your-customer rules for companies that rent out cloud computing
Liability insurance requirements for all frontier AI developers
ow: DNA screening targets bioweapon misuse.
Cloud KYC controls who can rent compute, mainly to enforce export controls.
Insurance helps pay for harms developers' models cause.

items.p: Suppose a few executives at a leading lab quietly use its most capable unreleased model for their own political or commercial advantage. Name two policy tools proposed to make this harder to do or easier to detect.
items.answer: Examples: logging and independent review of how lab leaders use internal models; tiered internal access rules and an internal-deployment oversight board; whistleblower protections for staff; security that holds even against the lab's own executives; public-interest board structures with attorney general oversight; embedded auditors.
keys: Logging and review of leadership's model use
Internal access rules or an oversight board
Whistleblower protections
Security that binds executives too
Public-interest governance or embedded auditors
items.x: This is the private-sector version of the 'many hands' problem: with a capable internal model, a few people need fewer staff to go along with them. Supporters of logging say records only work if they are tamper-resistant and reviewed by someone independent of the user.

choice.p: Which of these is a policy tool proposed to stop lab leaders from quietly using an internal model for their own advantage?
o: Tamper-resistant logs of executives' model use, reviewed by someone independent
Structural separation of chip, cloud and frontier model companies
Requiring government buyers to use several AI vendors
Public compute for university researchers to study frontier models
ow: Structural separation targets market concentration across chips, cloud and models; it doesn't watch what insiders do with a model.
Multi-vendor rules reduce government dependence on one firm; they don't constrain a lab's own executives.
Public compute widens outside research access; it doesn't monitor what insiders do.

items.p: Suppose AI makes it cheap for a government to monitor and sort huge numbers of people and act against them, work that once needed thousands of cooperating staff. Name two policy tools proposed to limit this.
items.answer: Examples: bans on particular uses, such as facial recognition by immigration agencies; requiring Congress to approve AI in criminal investigations, domestic intelligence and similar uses; process rules such as impact assessments, human review and appeals; logging government AI use as federal records, with audits; barring military AI from monitoring people in the US.
keys: Bans on specific uses
Congressional approval for protected uses
Process rules: impact assessments, human review, appeals
Logging and audits of government AI use
Ban on military AI surveillance at home
items.x: Supporters argue AI lowers the cost of watching and acting against people at scale, which erodes a practical check on abuse even before any law changes.
